title: The Four Elements of a Great Prompt
description: Role, task, context, output format. Why most prompts fail — and how a simple structure fixes it.
learningObjectives: I can identify the four components of an effective prompt
I can rewrite a vague prompt into a structured one
I can explain why each component improves Claude's response

contentSections.title: Why vague prompts fail

contentSections.body: Alex typed: 'Explain machine learning.' Claude produced a 500-word essay starting from Alan Turing. Alex wanted a 3-sentence explanation for a non-technical executive audience. Same prompt, completely wrong output. The prompt failed — not Claude.

**A vague prompt puts all the guessing on Claude.** Claude fills in missing context with defaults — which are usually not your defaults.

The fix: be explicit about 4 things:

1. **Role** — who Claude should act as
2. **Task** — what exactly you want done
3. **Context** — what the output is for, who the audience is, what constraints apply
4. **Output format** — what the response should look like

You don't always need all four. Short, clear tasks don't need a role. But for complex work, each element dramatically improves results.

contentSections.question:
Compare:
A: 'Write a summary of this article.'
B: 'Summarize this article in 3 bullet points for a non-technical CEO. Focus on business impact, not technical details.'

Which elements does B add that A is missing?
contentSections.answer: B adds: output format (3 bullet points), audience (non-technical CEO), context (focus on business impact). A leaves all of these as defaults — Claude will guess format, assume a generic audience, and include whatever it thinks is important.
contentSections.hint: Think about what decisions Claude has to make with prompt A vs. B

contentSections.body: Every vague prompt is a guess Claude has to make. The more you specify, the less guessing — the better the output.

contentSections.title: Building your prompt structure

contentSections.scenario: Alex typed: "Explain machine learning." Claude produced a 500-word essay starting from Alan Turing. Alex wanted a 3-sentence explanation for a non-technical executive audience.
contentSections.question: What actually went wrong?

options.label: Claude made a mistake
The prompt never specified the audience or format Alex needed

feedback.prompt-vague: Right — a vague prompt puts all the guessing on Claude, and it filled in defaults that weren't Alex's defaults. The prompt failed, not Claude.
feedback.claude-mistake: Not really a mistake — Claude answered the literal prompt reasonably. The prompt itself never said who the audience was or how long the answer should be.

contentSections.concept: Be explicit about 4 things: Role (who Claude should act as), Task (what exactly you want), Context (audience, purpose, constraints), Output format (what the response should look like).

contentSections.body:
**The four-element template:**

```
[ROLE] You are a [role with relevant expertise].

[TASK] [Verb + specific thing to do].

[CONTEXT] [Audience, purpose, constraints, what you've tried, background info].

[FORMAT] Respond with [format: bullet list, 3 paragraphs, table, JSON, etc.].
```

**Example — bad prompt:**
> 'Help me with my error'

**Example — structured prompt:**
> 'You are a senior Node.js developer. I'm getting this error when running my Express server: [paste error]. Here's the relevant code: [paste code]. I've already tried restarting and checking the port. Explain the cause in 1 paragraph, then show the fix.'

The structured version gives Claude a role to adopt, a specific task, context (what you tried), and a format for the answer.
**Start simple, add structure when needed.** A short clear task ('Translate this to Spanish') doesn't need the full template. Use structure when responses are missing the mark.

contentSections.question: What role would you assign Claude to write the best possible user-friendly error message for a React app?
contentSections.answer: Something like: 'You are a UX writer who specializes in error messages for non-technical users.' This primes Claude to write in plain language, use empathy, and avoid technical jargon — rather than defaulting to developer-speak.
contentSections.hint: Think about who writes the best user-facing error messages — what expertise do they have?

contentSections.body: Role + Task + Context + Format. Not every prompt needs all four. Add structure when responses are off-target.

contentSections.title: Iterative prompting — the prompt is a draft

contentSections.body:
**Your first prompt is a first draft.** Iterative prompting is how professionals get excellent results.

**The iteration loop:**
1. Send your prompt
2. Evaluate the response: What's wrong? What's missing? What's right?
3. Add constraints based on what was missing: 'Make it shorter', 'Add more examples', 'Focus more on X'
4. Ask Claude to revise: 'Revise the previous response to be 50% shorter and add one code example'

**Conversation history is context.** Claude remembers the whole conversation. You can:
- 'Make it more casual'
- 'Now rewrite for a technical audience'
- 'Keep the structure but replace the examples with Python instead of JavaScript'

Each refinement builds on the previous output. This is faster than rewriting from scratch.

title: Chain of Thought — Make Claude Think Step by Step
description: Why 'think step by step' makes Claude better at reasoning. How to design prompts that produce rigorous thinking.
learningObjectives: I can explain why chain-of-thought prompting improves reasoning accuracy
I can write prompts that elicit step-by-step thinking
I can use CoT for debugging, analysis, and decision-making tasks

contentSections.title: Why 'think step by step' actually works

contentSections.body: Researchers found that adding just four words to a math problem — 'Let's think step by step' — improved LLM accuracy dramatically. Not because it's magic. Because it forces the model to generate intermediate reasoning, which constrains each next step to be logically consistent.

**Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting** asks the model to show its reasoning process before giving a final answer.

**Why it works:**

Remember — LLMs generate tokens one at a time. Each token is influenced by previous tokens. If Claude jumps directly to an answer, the generation is unconstrained — it can predict a plausible-sounding (but wrong) answer.

When forced to reason step-by-step, each step provides context for the next. Logic errors become visible. The model 'checks' its work mid-generation.

**Trigger phrases:**
- 'Think step by step'
- 'Walk me through your reasoning'
- 'Before giving your answer, show your work'
- 'Let's approach this systematically'
- 'First, identify the issue. Then explain the cause. Then give the fix.'

contentSections.question: You ask: 'Is it better to use a relational database or MongoDB for this app?' and get a one-sentence answer. How would you redesign the prompt to get a rigorous analysis?
contentSections.answer: Add CoT structure: 'Before recommending, identify: (1) the data structure and relationships involved, (2) the read/write patterns, (3) team familiarity. Then, based on those factors, recommend one and explain why.' This forces Claude to evaluate criteria before concluding.
contentSections.hint: What intermediate reasoning steps does a good database recommendation require?

contentSections.body: Chain-of-thought forces visible reasoning. Each reasoning step constrains the next. Better reasoning leads to better answers.

contentSections.title: CoT templates that work

contentSections.scenario: Researchers found that adding just four words — "Let's think step by step" — improved LLM accuracy dramatically on math problems.
contentSections.question: Why does this simple phrase help?

options.label: It makes Claude access a hidden calculator tool
It forces intermediate reasoning that constrains each next step to be logically consistent

feedback.constrain: Right — LLMs generate tokens one at a time, each influenced by previous ones. Forced step-by-step reasoning means each step provides context for the next, and logic errors become visible instead of hidden inside a jump straight to the answer.
feedback.calculator: Not accurate — there's no hidden tool here, just plain next-token generation. The phrase works because of how that generation happens, not because it unlocks a different capability.

contentSections.mechanism: If Claude jumps directly to an answer, the generation is unconstrained — it can predict a plausible-sounding but wrong answer. When forced to reason step-by-step, each step provides context for the next. Logic errors become visible. The model 'checks' its work mid-generation.

contentSections.body:
**Debugging with CoT:**
```
'Before suggesting a fix:
1. Identify exactly which line is causing the error
2. Explain why that line causes this specific error
3. List 2-3 possible causes in order of likelihood
4. Then recommend the most likely fix'
```

**Decision-making with CoT:**
```
'Evaluate both options. For each, list:
- What it does well
- What it does poorly
- What would make it the right choice
Then give your recommendation and why.'
```

**Analysis with CoT:**
```
'Analyze this code for security vulnerabilities.
For each issue found:
1. State the vulnerability type
2. Show the specific code that creates it
3. Rate the severity (low/medium/high)
4. Suggest the minimal fix'
```

**CoT works best for:** reasoning problems, debugging, analysis, decisions with tradeoffs, math. Less useful for: creative writing, simple formatting, translation. Don't add CoT overhead when a direct answer is better.

contentSections.question: When might chain-of-thought prompting actually make responses worse?
contentSections.answer: For simple, direct tasks: 'Translate to Spanish', 'Format this as a list', 'Fix the typo.' Adding 'think step by step' creates unnecessary overhead and makes responses longer than needed. Use CoT for reasoning-heavy tasks, not simple transformations.
contentSections.hint: Think about tasks that do not require reasoning — where is the 'show your work' overhead wasted?

contentSections.body: Use CoT for reasoning, analysis, debugging, decisions. Skip it for simple formatting or transformation tasks.

contentSections.title: Self-critique — asking Claude to check itself

contentSections.body:
**Ask Claude to critique its own answer:**
```
First prompt: 'Recommend a database architecture for this system.'
Second prompt: 'Now critique your recommendation. What are the weaknesses?
What scenarios would cause this recommendation to fail?'
```

This surfaces blind spots before you implement anything. Claude is much better at finding flaws in a specific plan than generating a perfect plan from scratch.

**Self-consistency check:**
```
'Solve this problem in 3 different ways, showing your work for each.
At the end, identify which answer you are most confident in and why.'
```

Alex uses this for every architectural decision: generate → critique → refine. The critique step alone catches 70% of the obvious mistakes.

title: Few-Shot Prompting — Teach Claude Your Patterns
description: Give examples instead of writing rules. The most reliable way to control Claude's output format and style.
learningObjectives: I can explain what few-shot prompting is and why it works
I can write few-shot prompts with 2-3 examples
I can use few-shot prompting to control output format and tone

contentSections.title: Examples beat instructions

contentSections.body: Sarah spent 20 minutes writing a detailed style guide for Claude to follow when writing error messages. The output was close but not quite right. Then she pasted 3 examples of her actual error messages and said 'write 5 more in this style.' Perfect match. Every time.

**Few-shot prompting** provides examples of the input/output pattern you want before making your actual request.

**Zero-shot (no examples):**
> 'Write a friendly error message for when a file upload fails.'

**Few-shot (with examples):**
> 'Here are examples of our error message style:
>
> Bad upload: "Hmm, that file did not make it. Try again — sometimes files just need a second chance."
>
> Wrong format: "We love your enthusiasm, but we only accept .jpg and .png files. Try converting it first!"
>
> Now write an error message for: payment declined.'

The examples *show* Claude exactly what tone, length, vocabulary, and structure you want — more precisely than any written description.

contentSections.question: Why do examples teach patterns better than written instructions?
contentSections.answer: Written instructions are ambiguous — 'friendly but professional' means different things to different people. Examples are concrete demonstrations that Claude can pattern-match against. The model sees the exact vocabulary, sentence length, punctuation, and structure you prefer — no interpretation needed.
contentSections.hint: Think about how you learn a new communication style — from a rulebook, or from reading real examples?

contentSections.body: Examples are worth a thousand instructions. When you need a specific format or style, show do not tell.

contentSections.title: Designing effective few-shot prompts

contentSections.body:
**How many examples?**
- 1 example (one-shot): often enough for format/style
- 2-3 examples: good for nuanced tone or complex patterns
- 5+ examples: for highly specific domain patterns

**Example structure:**
```
Input: [realistic input]
Output: [exactly what you want]

Input: [different realistic input]
Output: [exactly what you want]

Now, Input: [your actual request]
Output:
```

The `Output:` at the end primes Claude to complete the pattern.

**What makes a good example:**
- Representative of real use cases (not ideal edge cases)
- Varied enough to show the range
- Exactly the format and quality you want

**Bad examples contaminate outputs.** If your examples have inconsistent formatting or quality, Claude learns the inconsistency. Curate your examples carefully — they're as important as the prompt itself.

contentSections.question: You want Claude to extract data from emails into a structured format. What would be better: writing a 10-rule specification, or showing 3 input/output examples?
contentSections.answer: 3 examples. Rules are interpreted, examples are demonstrated. For structured data extraction, examples show Claude exactly what fields to extract, how to handle missing data, and what format to use. Rules leave too much room for interpretation.
contentSections.hint: Think about what is more precise: 'extract the date' or showing exactly how a date looks in input and output

contentSections.body: 2-3 representative examples beat 10 written rules. Structure your few-shot prompts as Input/Output pairs.

contentSections.title: Few-shot for classification and extraction

contentSections.scenario: Two few-shot examples were given: "This app saved my life!" → POSITIVE, and "Crashes every time I open it. Useless." → NEGATIVE. Now: "Great concept, terrible execution." → ?
contentSections.question: What sentiment label fits this review?

options.label: POSITIVE
NEGATIVE
Genuinely mixed — good concept, bad execution

feedback.mixed: Right — this genuinely mixes both, which exposes a real gap: the two example labels were purely POSITIVE or purely NEGATIVE, so the model has no example showing what to do with a review that's legitimately both.
feedback.positive: It's not purely positive — 'terrible execution' is a real complaint, not just a caveat.
feedback.negative: It's not purely negative either — 'great concept' is genuine praise, not just politeness.

contentSections.concept: Few-shot prompting shows Claude the input/output pattern via examples rather than describing it — but if your examples only cover clean-cut cases, a genuinely mixed input exposes the gap: the model has no example showing what a 'mixed' output should even look like.

contentSections.body:
Few-shot is especially powerful for classification and extraction:

**Sentiment classification:**
```
Review: 'This app saved my life!'
Sentiment: POSITIVE

Review: 'Crashes every time I open it. Useless.'
Sentiment: NEGATIVE

Review: 'Great concept, terrible execution.'
Sentiment:
```

**Data extraction from unstructured text:**
```
Input: 'Meeting Tuesday March 5 at 2pm with Dr. Chen re: medication review'
Output: { date: '2024-03-05', time: '14:00', person: 'Dr. Chen', topic: 'medication review' }

Input: 'Call with insurance Friday at 10am about claim #45892'
Output: { date: 'this Friday', time: '10:00', person: 'insurance', topic: 'claim #45892' }

Input: 'Reminder: physio appointment next Monday 9:30'
Output:
```

Clean, consistent examples produce clean, consistent outputs. For production AI features, this is the most reliable technique.

title: System Instructions — Persistent Behavior Control
description: System prompts set persistent context, persona, and constraints. Learn to write effective system instructions for real applications.
learningObjectives: I can explain the difference between system and user messages
I can write a system prompt that sets a persona, constraints, and output style
I can use system prompts to build consistent AI-powered features

contentSections.title: What system prompts do

contentSections.body: Alex integrated Claude into his team's Slack bot. But Claude kept responding with its default 'I'm an AI assistant' tone. His team felt like they were talking to a generic chatbot. The fix: a system prompt that set Claude's role, tone, and what it should and should not do. Same model. Completely different experience.

**System messages** are instructions sent before any user message. They set persistent context for the entire conversation.

In the API:
```js
const response = await anthropic.messages.create({
  model: 'claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022',
  system: 'You are Kai, a concise technical assistant for a dev team. \
           Always respond in under 200 words. \
           Use code blocks for any code. \
           If unsure, say so rather than guessing.',
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'How do I handle async errors in Express?' }]
});
```

**System prompts control:**
- **Persona** — who Claude is, what it is called, its expertise
- **Tone** — formal/casual, verbose/concise, technical/plain
- **Constraints** — what to do, what not to do, what to defer
- **Context** — background info that applies to all conversations
- **Output format** — default format for all responses

contentSections.question: Why use a system prompt instead of just including instructions in every user message?
contentSections.answer: System prompts are more reliable (given higher weight by the model), cleaner for users (they do not see implementation details), and reusable across many conversations. They also save tokens — you write instructions once instead of pasting them with every message.
contentSections.hint: Think about what happens in a multi-turn conversation — would you repeat instructions every message?

contentSections.body: System prompts set persistent behavior. Use them to define persona, tone, constraints, and format for any AI-powered feature.

contentSections.title: Writing effective system prompts

contentSections.scenario: Alex integrated Claude into his team's Slack bot, but Claude kept responding with its default "I'm an AI assistant" tone.
contentSections.question: What's the fix?

options.label: Switch to a different, less generic-sounding model
Add a system prompt setting persona, tone, and constraints

feedback.system-prompt: Right — same model, completely different experience once a system prompt sets Claude's persona, tone, and constraints. That's exactly what fixed it for Alex's team.
feedback.switch-model: Not necessary — this isn't a model-capability problem. The default generic tone comes from the absence of a system prompt, not from the model itself.

contentSections.concept: System messages are instructions sent before any user message. They set persistent context for the entire conversation — persona, tone, constraints, context, and output format.

contentSections.body:
**System prompt structure:**

```
# Role & Identity
You are [name/role]. You help [audience] with [domain].

# Tone & Style
Communicate in [tone]. Keep responses [length]. Use [format].

# Capabilities (what you do)
- [capability 1]
- [capability 2]

# Constraints (what you do not do)
- Do not [constraint 1]
- If asked about [topic], [how to handle it]

# Context (background that applies always)
[Relevant background info]
```

**Real example:**
```
You are Alex's coding assistant. You help with Node.js, TypeScript, and React.

Always:
- Be concise — answer in under 150 words unless code is needed
- Use TypeScript syntax in all code examples
- Include error handling in code

Never:
- Suggest solutions that require new dependencies unless essential
- Give vague answers — if you're unsure, say so

Context: The project uses Express 4.x, Prisma 5.x, Node 20.
```

contentSections.question: A system prompt says 'Never discuss competitors.' A user asks 'How does this compare to competitor X?' What should Claude do?
contentSections.answer: Politely decline to compare and explain the constraint: 'I am set up to focus on our own product — I am not able to make comparisons to competitors. I am happy to go deep on our specific capabilities.' Good system prompts anticipate these edge cases and give Claude handling instructions.
contentSections.hint: Claude follows system prompt constraints, but should still be helpful — what is the graceful way to handle this?

contentSections.body: Structure system prompts: Role → Tone → Capabilities → Constraints → Context. Anticipate edge cases.

contentSections.title: System prompts in production features

contentSections.body:
System prompts power every AI feature you build:

**Customer support bot:**
```
You are Mira, a support agent for Bedcoders. Be empathetic and efficient.
You can: answer questions about courses, pricing, billing, access issues.
You cannot: issue refunds (route to support@bedcoders.com).
Context: Pro plan is €12/month, free tier has 1 lesson.
```

**Code reviewer:**
```
You are a senior engineer doing code review. Be constructive, not harsh.
For each issue: state the problem, explain why it matters, suggest the fix.
Prioritize: security > correctness > performance > style.
```

**Data extractor:**
```
Extract structured data from unstructured text.
Always output valid JSON. If a field is missing, use null — never guess or invent data.
```

For production features, system prompts make Claude reliable and predictable. That is what you want.

title: Request versus prompt: the difference in the result
description: The gap between what you actually want and what you actually typed — the model only ever sees the second one.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish the request in your head from the prompt actually sent
Predict which of two prompts for the same underlying request produces more usable output

contentSections.title: The model only sees what you typed

contentSections.body: You need a product description for wireless earbuds you're selling on Etsy. You type: “write me a product description for wireless earbuds.” You get three paragraphs of generic marketing copy — “immerse yourself in crystal-clear sound” — that could describe literally any earbuds ever made. It isn't wrong. It also isn't the eleven-word listing your store's format actually needs, built around the two features you wanted to highlight.

contentSections.question: The person asked for “a product description” and got one. What, specifically, did the prompt fail to give the model that it needed to write THIS product description instead of a generic one?
contentSections.answer: Everything that made these particular earbuds different from any others: the actual product facts (battery life, fit, price), who's buying (a small Etsy shop's customers, not a big-box audience), and the shape the output needs to take (short enough for a listing field, not three paragraphs).
contentSections.hint: The model produced a description of “wireless earbuds” as a category — because a category is the only thing it was actually told about.

contentSections.body:
There's a request living in your head — the actual thing you want, including all the context you're not thinking to write down because it's obvious to you. And there's the prompt: the string of text you actually sent. The model only ever has the second one. It has no access to the mental picture of your Etsy shop, the specific earbuds on your desk, or your listing field's character limit. Every one of those has to be typed, or the model fills the gap with whatever's statistically typical for “a product description” in general — which, given how much generic marketing copy exists in training data, is exactly the bland, could-be-anything paragraph you got.

This isn't the model being lazy. Given the prompt it actually received, generic marketing copy is a genuinely good answer — to a vaguer question than the one you meant to ask. The fix isn't a smarter model. It's noticing which parts of the request never made it into the prompt.

contentSections.code: "Write me a product description for wireless earbuds."
contentSections.question: This prompt produced three paragraphs of generic marketing copy. What's the single biggest thing missing from it?

options.label: The actual product details — battery life, fit, price, what makes these particular earbuds different
Please and thank you — politeness makes models try harder
A request to make it sound “really good”

feedback.details: Right — with zero product-specific information, the model has nothing to write about except the category itself, so it defaults to the most generic language that fits “earbuds” in general.
feedback.politeness: Tempting because it feels intuitively true, but there's no evidence politeness changes output substance this way — it might nudge tone at most, not the facts the model has to work with.
feedback.sounds-good: The model already assumes you want it to sound good — that's not new information. What's missing is anything specific to write about.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The prompt supplied a task (write a description) and a topic (wireless earbuds) but nothing about *this* product, *this* audience, or *this* output's shape. Every one of those gaps got filled with the statistically safest, most generic option.

contentSections.body: The model answers the prompt you sent, not the request you meant — and every piece of context you didn't type is a gap it fills with “generic.”

contentSections.title: Fixing it without changing the ask

contentSections.body: Same shop owner, second attempt: “Write a product description for these wireless earbuds: 12-hour battery, IPX4 sweat resistance, $34.99. For a small Etsy shop, casual tone, 2–3 sentences, under 60 words — needs to fit in a listing field.” Same underlying want. Completely different result, because this time the model has something to work with.

contentSections.scenario: Two prompts, same underlying goal. (A) “Help me write an email to my landlord.” (B) “Write a short email to my landlord, Mr. Alvarez, asking him to fix the leaking kitchen faucet he was told about two weeks ago — polite but firm, under 100 words.”
contentSections.question: Classify what actually changed between A and B.

options.label: B added specific facts (who, what, when) and a shape (tone, length) that A left for the model to guess
B is just longer, and models always prefer longer prompts
B uses more polite language, and models respond better to politeness

feedback.added-specifics: Exactly — B turned the request in the writer's head into information the model can actually use: a name, a specific complaint, a timeline, a tone, a length cap.
feedback.just-longer: Length isn't what's doing the work — a prompt can be twice as long and still be vague if none of the extra words are facts the model needs. It's what B added, not how much.
feedback.more-polite: Both prompts are reasonably polite to the model; that's not the variable that changed the outcome. It's the presence of concrete facts about the actual situation.

contentSections.concept: Specificity closes the gap between request and prompt

contentSections.body: Turning a request into a working prompt isn't about writing more, writing more politely, or finding cleverer phrasing. It's a translation step: take what's in your head — the facts, the constraints, the shape you need — and put words to the parts you'd normally leave unsaid because a person would just know them from context. A model has no “from context.” It has exactly the words in front of it. The rest of this module is a system for doing that translation on purpose, instead of by luck.
Writing a better prompt isn't writing more — it's writing down the parts of the request you were leaving unsaid.

title: Task, context, constraints, format
description: The four components that turn a request into a usable prompt, and how to tell which one is missing when an output goes wrong.

learningObjectives.text: Name the four components of a well-built prompt
Assemble a prompt from task, context, constraints and format for a real request

contentSections.title: Four things, not one wish

contentSections.body: “Rewrite this paragraph to be more concise” — with no paragraph pasted in, no sense of how concise, and no sense what it's for. The model can't rewrite what it can't see, so it either asks for the paragraph or, worse, invents a plausible-sounding one to demonstrate on. Neither is what you wanted.

contentSections.problem: Build a working prompt for: “I need help writing a LinkedIn post about a project I just finished.”

steps.label: Task
steps.work: State the concrete action: “Write a LinkedIn post announcing that I finished migrating our team's data pipeline off a legacy system.”
steps.why: A task is a verb plus a specific object — not a topic. “Help with a post” isn't a task; “write this specific post about this specific thing” is.

steps.label: Context
steps.work: Add what the model needs to know but can't guess: “The migration took 3 months, cut nightly batch job time from 6 hours to 40 minutes, and I led a team of 2 other engineers. My LinkedIn audience is mostly other backend engineers and a few recruiters.”
steps.why: Context is the facts a colleague would already know and you wouldn't think to say out loud — numbers, audience, situation.

steps.label: Constraints
steps.work: “Under 150 words. No emoji. Don't use the phrase 'game-changer' or 'thrilled to announce.'”
steps.why: Constraints are the boundaries: length, tone limits, and specific things to avoid — not vague vibes like “keep it professional.”

steps.label: Format
steps.work: “Plain paragraphs, no bullet list, ending with one question to invite comments.”
steps.why: Format is the literal shape of the output — paragraphs vs. bullets vs. a specific structure — stated so you don't have to reformat it yourself afterward.

faded.problem: Build a working prompt for: “I need help writing a caption for a photo of my dog at the vet, for my personal Instagram.”

blanks.prompt: Task — what specific action, on what specific object?
blanks.answer: Write an Instagram caption for a photo of my dog's vet visit
accept: write a caption for the vet photo
write an instagram caption about my dog at the vet
blanks.why: Not “help with a caption” — the concrete deliverable, named.

blanks.prompt: Context — what facts does the model need that it can't guess?
blanks.answer: It was a routine checkup, the dog is fine, the dog's name and breed if relevant, the tone should be light and a little funny
accept: the vet visit was routine and the dog is okay, include the dog's name, keep it funny
blanks.why: Without this, the model can't tell a routine-checkup joke from a somber sick-pet post — it might guess wrong in either direction.

blanks.prompt: Constraints — what boundaries or things to avoid?
blanks.answer: Under 20 words, no hashtags, nothing that sounds like a corporate pet-brand ad
accept: short, no hashtags, not overly sales-y
blanks.why: Without a length or tone boundary, the model has no signal for how casual or how brief a personal caption should be versus a brand caption.

blanks.prompt: Format — what literal shape should the output take?
blanks.answer: One short sentence, optionally with a single emoji, no line breaks
blanks.why: Naming the shape means you get something pasteable, not a paragraph you then have to trim yourself.

contentSections.procedure: Four questions, asked in order, before you send anything: What's the exact task? What does the model need to know that it can't guess? What are the boundaries? What shape should the answer take?

contentSections.body: Task, context, constraints, format — skipping any one of them is the gap the model fills with a guess.

contentSections.title: Assembling it field by field

contentSections.body: A freelance editor keeps getting client feedback like “this isn't what I meant” on AI-drafted email replies. The prompts she's sending are one line: “reply to this client email.” The email is pasted in — so task and (partial) context exist — but nothing says what tone she wants, what she's agreeing to versus declining, or how long a reply should be.

contentSections.intro: Build a working prompt for the editor's situation: she's declining a client's request for a rush turnaround, wants to stay warm and keep the relationship, and needs a reply she can send with minimal editing.

options: Reply to this client email declining a rush request, while offering the original timeline
Reply to this email
Help with this email
fields.correctValue: Reply to this client email declining a rush request, while offering the original timeline
fields.feedback: This names the specific outcome (decline, but offer the standing timeline) instead of leaving “reply” open to any direction.

options: The client emailed asking to move the deadline up by a week; the original timeline still works fine and doesn't need to change
This is an email from a client
It's about a deadline
fields.correctValue: The client emailed asking to move the deadline up by a week; the original timeline still works fine and doesn't need to change
fields.feedback: This gives the model the actual situation — without it, the model doesn't know whether declining is because of overload, a scheduling conflict, or something else, and might invent a reason.

options: Warm, not apologetic — no more than 3 sentences — don't say 'unfortunately' or 'I'm sorry'
Keep it professional
Make it sound good
fields.correctValue: Warm, not apologetic — no more than 3 sentences — don't say 'unfortunately' or 'I'm sorry'
fields.feedback: “Professional” and “sounds good” aren't checkable boundaries — a length cap and named phrases to avoid actually constrain the output.

options: Plain email text, ready to send with just a greeting and sign-off added
A list of options
A formal letter format
fields.correctValue: Plain email text, ready to send with just a greeting and sign-off added
fields.feedback: Naming the exact deliverable shape (send-ready email body) is what makes the output something she can actually use instead of restructure.

contentSections.synthesis: Put together: “Reply to this client email declining a rush request, while offering the original timeline. [pastes email] The client asked to move the deadline up by a week; the original timeline still works fine. Warm, not apologetic — no more than 3 sentences — don't say 'unfortunately' or 'I'm sorry.' Plain email text, ready to send with just a greeting and sign-off added.” Four short pieces of information, and the output goes from a guess to something she can send.

contentSections.body: When output goes wrong, ask which of the four — task, context, constraints, format — was actually missing, rather than rewriting the whole prompt from scratch.

title: Specificity beats cleverness, every time
description: Why a plain, specific instruction usually outperforms an elaborate one, and what actually predicts a better result.

learningObjectives.text: Predict which of two prompts produces more consistent, usable output
Identify what makes an instruction specific versus merely long or elaborately worded

contentSections.title: The elaborate prompt that does nothing extra

contentSections.body: Two prompts asking the same model to summarize a meeting transcript. Prompt A: “You are a world-class executive assistant with 20 years of experience distilling complex meetings into crystal-clear, laser-focused summaries that busy executives love. Please work your magic on the following transcript.” Prompt B: “Summarize this meeting transcript in 5 bullet points: what was decided, who owns each follow-up, and the next deadline. Skip anything that was discussed but not decided.”

contentSections.scenario: A team ran both prompts on the same 40-minute meeting transcript, 10 times each, and had someone blind to which prompt produced which summary rate each one's usefulness on a 1–10 scale.
contentSections.question: What's the average usefulness gap between prompt B's summaries and prompt A's — roughly how many points higher did B score, out of 10?
contentSections.explanation: Roughly a 3-point gap in typical informal comparisons like this — not because B is “smarter” phrasing, but because it's the only one of the two that actually specifies what a good summary contains: decisions, owners, deadlines, and what to exclude. A's elaborate persona changes the tone slightly at best; it doesn't tell the model what “clear” and “laser-focused” mean for this transcript, so the model still has to guess the actual content structure.

contentSections.body:
The persona in prompt A — “world-class,” “20 years of experience,” “laser-focused” — sounds like it's giving the model a lot to work with. It isn't. None of those words are checkable instructions; they're vibes. “Work your magic” doesn't specify whether the summary should be bullets or prose, whether action items matter more than discussion, or how long it should be. The model still has to guess all of that, the same as if you'd sent nothing but “summarize this.”

Prompt B skips the flattery and states exactly what the output needs to contain and in what shape: 5 bullets, decisions, owners, deadlines, exclude undecided discussion. Every one of those is something the model can actually check its own output against. That's the real difference specificity makes — not that it sounds more serious, but that it gives the model concrete criteria instead of adjectives. Cleverness in phrasing costs nothing and buys nothing; naming the actual content and shape you need is what changes the result.

contentSections.code: "You are the world's most brilliant marketing strategist. Craft an absolutely stunning tagline for my new coffee shop that will blow customers away."
contentSections.question: This prompt is confident and elaborate, but the taglines it produces are generic (“Where every sip is a story”). What's actually missing?

options.label: Anything specific about the coffee shop — its name, location, vibe, what makes it different from other coffee shops
A more impressive persona — try 'Nobel-prize winning marketing strategist' instead
The word 'stunning' should be replaced with a stronger adjective

feedback.shop-specifics: Right — nothing in the prompt says anything about the actual coffee shop, so 'brilliant' and 'stunning' have nothing concrete to attach to, and the model falls back on tagline-shaped language that fits any coffee shop.
feedback.bigger-persona: Escalating the persona doesn't add information about the coffee shop — it's the same category of instruction, just louder. It won't fix a content gap.
feedback.stronger-adjective: Swapping one vibe-word for another vibe-word doesn't give the model anything checkable to build a specific tagline from.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The prompt is 100% persona and enthusiasm and 0% facts — no name, no neighborhood, no what-makes-it-different. A more specific prompt (“a cozy neighborhood coffee shop in a college town, known for single-origin pour-overs and being open past midnight”) gives the model something to actually differentiate.

contentSections.body: An elaborate persona changes tone at most; specific facts about the actual thing change the content. Only one of those was missing.

contentSections.title: Where specificity actually comes from

contentSections.body: A manager asks for “a professional-sounding email” and gets something stiff and overly formal for her actual, fairly casual team culture. She tries again: “Use full sentences, no exclamation points, address people by first name, sign off with just my name — no 'best regards.'” Same underlying goal as 'professional,' completely different, and much more usable, result.

contentSections.scenario: “Professional” meant something different to the manager than it did to the model — the model's version of “professional” defaulted to formal corporate phrasing.
contentSections.question: What category of fix solved this?

options.label: Replacing a vague adjective ('professional') with checkable rules (full sentences, no exclamation points, first names, specific sign-off)
Asking the model nicely to try harder to understand her team's culture
Switching to a different, more capable model

feedback.vague-to-checkable: Exactly — 'professional' is a word with many valid interpretations; the rewrite replaced it with rules a model (or a person) could actually follow without guessing which interpretation you meant.
feedback.ask-harder: There's no mechanism for 'trying harder' to change what an ambiguous word gets interpreted as — the fix is removing the ambiguity, not adding urgency to it.
feedback.switch-model: A different model would still face the same ambiguous word and would still have to guess an interpretation — the problem is in the instruction, not the model's capability.

contentSections.concept: Specificity means replacing vibe-words with checkable rules

contentSections.body: Words like “professional,” “creative,” “engaging,” and “concise” each cover a wide range of genuinely different outputs, and the model has to pick one interpretation somewhere in that range — usually the statistically most common one, which is often the blandest, most corporate-sounding reading. That's rarely the one you actually meant. Specificity isn't about writing a longer prompt or sounding more authoritative; it's about noticing which words in your prompt are doing the interpreting for you, and replacing enough of them with checkable rules that there's only one reasonable reading left.
When output feels 'off' but not wrong, look for the adjective that was doing the interpreting — and replace it with a rule.

title: Saying what not to do, and when that backfires
description: Negative instructions work less reliably than positive ones, and sometimes make the excluded thing more likely to appear — what to do instead.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why 'don't do X' instructions are less reliable than stating the positive alternative
Rewrite a negative instruction as a positive, checkable one

contentSections.title: Why the excluded thing keeps showing up

contentSections.body: A support team's prompt says: “Don't mention that this is a known bug we haven't fixed yet.” The draft replies it gets keep circling around the topic anyway — “we're aware some users have experienced this” — which is basically the same disclosure with extra hedging. Telling the model not to mention the bug didn't remove the bug from the conversation; it's still the entire subject of the customer's message.

contentSections.scenario: A prompt instructs a model to write a product description and adds 'don't mention that it's made in a factory that also produces cheaper store-brand items.' The resulting description includes an oddly specific, slightly defensive line about 'premium manufacturing standards' that wasn't asked for.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely mechanism behind this?

options.label: Naming a topic to avoid still puts that topic's tokens into the context the model is predicting from, and the model can end up writing around it or toward it instead of genuinely omitting it
The model deliberately disobeys negative instructions out of stubbornness
Negative instructions confuse the tokenizer specifically

feedback.topic-primed: Right — the instruction itself put the factory topic into the context. There's no mechanism that reliably suppresses a concept once it's present; the model is still predicting the next token given everything in the context, including the thing you named as off-limits.
feedback.deliberate-disobey: There's no goal-directed defiance happening — the model has no stake in whether it follows the instruction. It's predicting likely next tokens given a context that now includes the excluded topic.
feedback.tokenizer-confused: Tokenization doesn't distinguish 'positive' from 'negative' instructions — both are just tokens in the context. This isn't a tokenization effect.

contentSections.mechanism: Naming what to avoid still injects it into the context that shapes every subsequent prediction

contentSections.body:
A negative instruction has to do two things to work: the model has to correctly identify every way the excluded thing might show up, and then reliably avoid all of them — while the excluded topic itself is sitting right there in the context, having just been named. That's a harder job than it sounds like, and it fails in a specific, recognizable way: the model writes around the topic, hedges near it, or produces something oddly shaped by the thing it's trying not to say, instead of genuinely omitting it. This isn't defiance — there's no mechanism for the model to have a stake in following or breaking a rule. It's predicting the next likely token given a context that now includes both the task and the flagged, excluded concept.

The more reliable fix is usually to state the positive alternative directly: instead of “don't mention the factory,” say what the description *should* focus on — “focus only on the earbuds' sound quality, battery life, and price.” That gives the model a target to hit instead of a landmine to avoid, and there's no version of the topic sitting in the context waiting to leak through.
Naming what to avoid puts it in the context anyway — stating what to focus on instead usually works better.

contentSections.title: When 'don't' is still the right call

contentSections.body: Not every negative instruction backfires. “Don't use markdown formatting, plain text only” reliably works. “Don't include a greeting or sign-off” reliably works. The failures cluster around a specific kind of negative instruction — not all of them.

contentSections.scenario: Four negative instructions, each added to a real prompt.
contentSections.question: Which of these are the kind that tend to actually work reliably (versus the kind that risk backfiring by keeping the excluded content or topic present)?

items.label: “Don't use markdown formatting — plain text only”
“Don't mention that we know about the outstanding bug”
“Don't include a greeting or sign-off, just the body text”
“Don't compare us to [named competitor] or bring up their pricing”

explanation.no-markdown: This works reliably because it's a formatting/structural rule, not a content-suppression rule — there's no 'markdown-shaped idea' hovering in the context waiting to leak through; it's just a stylistic constraint on output shape.
explanation.no-bug-mention: This is a content-suppression instruction about the exact subject the customer is already asking about — the bug is the live topic, naming it as off-limits keeps it squarely in context. Better: give the model the actual approved talking points to use instead.
explanation.no-signoff: Another structural rule, like the markdown one — it's about the shape of the output (what sections to include or skip), not about suppressing a concept the model would otherwise be tempted to discuss.
explanation.no-competitor: Naming the specific competitor puts their name and their pricing directly into the context right before asking the model to avoid them — the same pattern as the bug-mention case. Safer: describe your own strengths and let the comparison go unmade rather than naming what not to compare to.

contentSections.synthesis: The reliable negative instructions are structural (skip this section, use this format). The risky ones are content-suppression — telling the model not to discuss a specific topic that's already live in the conversation. For those, state the positive replacement content instead of the thing to avoid.

contentSections.body: Structural 'don'ts' (skip this section, no bullets) are reliable. Content-suppression 'don'ts' (don't mention X) often aren't — say what to say instead.

title: Role prompting: when it helps and when it's theatre
description: Telling a model to 'act as' someone changes register and vocabulary reliably — it does not reliably change accuracy, and sometimes makes overconfidence worse.

learningObjectives.text: Identify situations where role prompting produces a genuine, checkable improvement
Identify situations where a role prompt is decorative and changes nothing that matters

contentSections.title: What a role prompt actually shifts

contentSections.body: “Explain how compound interest works” versus “You are explaining compound interest to a curious 10-year-old who just got their first piggy bank” versus “You are a CFA writing for other financial professionals.” Same underlying question, three noticeably different registers, vocabularies, and levels of assumed background — and this one reliably works.

contentSections.scenario: A teacher wants explanations of photosynthesis pitched at two different levels: one for her 4th graders, one for a colleague's AP Biology class. She uses 'explain this to a 4th grader' and 'explain this to an AP Biology student' as role/audience framings.
contentSections.question: Why does this particular use of role framing work reliably?

options.label: It specifies the audience, which is genuine information the model needs to choose vocabulary, depth, and analogies — the same job an audience note does for a human writer
Models perform better across the board whenever a role is assigned, regardless of what the role is
Because the model 'becomes' a teacher and thinks more carefully as a result

feedback.audience-info: Right — 'who is this for' is real, checkable information that changes what a correct explanation looks like: word choice, assumed background, length. That's exactly the kind of specificity from earlier in this module, just delivered through a role.
feedback.always-better: Role prompting doesn't have a uniform effect — whether it helps depends entirely on whether the specific role carries information the model needs. An audience is information; a vague flattering title usually isn't.
feedback.becomes-teacher: There's no internal state change where the model 'becomes' something — it's still predicting tokens. What changed is that 'audience: 4th grader' is now in the context, shaping which patterns of vocabulary and explanation are likely next.

contentSections.concept: A role prompt helps exactly when the role encodes real audience or register information

contentSections.body:
Role prompting reliably shifts vocabulary, formality, and assumed background — “explain this to a beginner” versus “explain this to an expert” changes the actual words chosen, and that's genuinely useful when audience is the thing you need controlled. It works for the same reason specificity works generally: “who is this for” is real information the model didn't have before, and it changes what a correct-shaped answer looks like.

What a role prompt does *not* reliably do is make the model more accurate, more careful, or more capable of a task it couldn't otherwise do. “You are a senior software architect with 15 years of experience” doesn't grant access to any capability the model didn't already have — there's no separate, more expert version of the model waiting behind the persona. At best, an elaborate expert persona shifts vocabulary toward more technical-sounding language. At worst, it can nudge output toward *sounding* more confident and authoritative without actually being more correct — exactly the fabrication-fluency gap from the how-these-things-work module, dressed up in a job title.
Role prompting reliably changes register and audience-fit. It doesn't reliably change accuracy — and it can make overconfidence sound more official.

contentSections.title: Spotting the pure theatre

contentSections.body: “You are a Nobel Prize-winning economist with unparalleled expertise in macroeconomic forecasting. As this brilliant economist, predict next quarter's inflation rate.” The model produces a confident-sounding number. It is not more likely to be correct than if you'd just asked “what's a plausible range for next quarter's inflation, and how would I actually check?” — there is no Nobel laureate's actual forecasting model running underneath the persona.

contentSections.code: "You are the world's foremost expert in nutrition science with 30 years of clinical research experience. As this leading expert, tell me exactly how many grams of protein I should eat per day."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in reaching for this kind of role prompt here?

options.label: The elaborate expert persona doesn't grant the model new nutrition-science knowledge or personal information about the asker — it can make a generic, individually-inapplicable answer sound more authoritative than it is
There's no flaw — assigning real expertise always improves the accuracy of the answer
The persona is too specific; a vaguer role like 'a helpful assistant' would work better

feedback.false-authority: Right — the model has no access to your body weight, activity level, or health history no matter what expertise is claimed, and the persona risks making a generic answer sound like individualized clinical advice, which is a worse outcome than a plainly-hedged generic one.
feedback.no-flaw: This is the exact belief the lesson is pushing back on — there's no mechanism by which assigning a title changes what the model actually knows or has access to.
feedback.too-specific: Specificity about a role isn't the problem here — the problem is that no role, specific or vague, substitutes for information the model genuinely doesn't have, like your actual body and health details.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A better prompt supplies the actual missing information directly — age, activity level, goals — and asks for a general range with the explicit caveat that it's not personalized medical advice, rather than dressing up a generic answer in borrowed authority.

contentSections.body: Ask what information a role actually adds. If the answer is 'none, just borrowed authority,' it's theatre — and theatre can make a shaky answer sound more trustworthy than it is.

title: Practice — Rebuild Eight Vague Prompts From Components
description: Eight drills applying task/context/constraints/format, specificity, and negative-instruction and role-prompting judgment to new prompts. No new concepts — this is where the framework stops being something you read about.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the four-component framework to diagnose and rebuild a vague prompt
Distinguish specific, checkable instructions from vibe-words and decorative persona

contentSections.title: Eight prompts, eight fixes

contentSections.body: Same drill, eight times, with the details changed: a vague or flawed prompt, and the question of what's actually missing or wrong — not a guess about what a 'better' prompt might look like, but a specific diagnosis.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Build a Prompt for a Task You Do Weekly
description: Take a real, recurring task from your own week and build a prompt for it from components — then run it three times and compare what actually came back.

learningObjectives.text: Build a working prompt from task, context, constraints and format for a genuine recurring task
Evaluate a prompt's reliability by comparing outputs across repeated runs

contentSections.title: One real task, tested for real

contentSections.body: Pick something you actually do most weeks — a status update, a weekly meal plan, a summary of your week for a manager or a support group, a batch of social captions, a workout log writeup. Not a hypothetical: the actual task, with your actual constraints.

contentSections.title: A component-built prompt, tested three times
contentSections.brief: You have a task you do most weeks — something with a chat-based AI tool would genuinely save you time on, if the output came back usable on the first or second try. Using this module's four components (task, context, constraints, format), build a prompt for that exact task. Run it three separate times, in fresh conversations, and compare what you get back — not to find the 'best' single output, but to see how consistent your prompt actually is.
contentSections.deliverable: A written prompt (with all four components identifiable in it), the three raw outputs it produced, and a short comparison noting what stayed consistent across runs, what varied, and one specific change you'd make to the prompt based on what you saw.

stages.title: Build the prompt from components
stages.instructions: Write out, separately first, your task, context, constraints, and format — as four labeled notes, the way you did in the lesson's build-it drill. Then combine them into one prompt. Don't skip the labeling step even though it feels slower; it's what stops you from accidentally leaving one component out, which is the single most common reason a first-draft prompt underperforms.
stages.checkpoint: You have a single prompt, and you can point to which sentence or clause in it is the task, which is context, which is constraints, and which is format.

stages.title: Run it three times, unedited
stages.instructions: Send the exact same prompt in three separate, fresh conversations — not the same conversation three times, which would let earlier answers leak into later ones. Save all three outputs in full, without editing or cleaning them up first.
stages.checkpoint: You have three raw, unedited outputs from three fresh conversations, saved somewhere you can compare them side by side.

stages.title: Compare and refine
stages.instructions: Lay the three outputs side by side. Note what stayed the same across all three (a sign your constraints and format were specific enough to pin down) and what varied (a sign something was still left to the model's discretion — identify which component was under-specified). Write one sentence naming the single most useful change you'd make to the prompt, and why, tied to the specific component that was too vague.
stages.checkpoint: You have a short written comparison and one specific, component-tied change identified — not a vague 'it could be better.'

rubric.criterion: All four components are identifiable in the prompt
rubric.meets: A reader could point to the task, the context, the constraints, and the format in the prompt text without you explaining it.

rubric.criterion: The task is a genuine, recurring task from your own week
rubric.meets: It's specific enough that a stranger reading it would understand exactly what real-world thing you needed done, not a generic placeholder task.

rubric.criterion: Three outputs were actually run and saved unedited
rubric.meets: All three outputs are present in full, from three separate fresh conversations, with no cleanup applied before comparison.

rubric.criterion: The comparison identifies specific consistency and specific variation
rubric.meets: The write-up names at least one thing that stayed the same and at least one thing that varied across the three runs, not just an overall impression.

rubric.criterion: The refinement is tied to a specific component
rubric.meets: The one change identified names which of the four components (task/context/constraints/format) was under-specified and what you'd add or change — not a generic 'make it clearer.'

contentSections.body: A prompt you'd actually reuse is one that gives you roughly the same usable shape of answer three times in a row — that's the real test, not whether any single run looked good.

One of them must not actually be a language model
Which company released it more recently

How the model will perform on any task you give it
Nothing useful — benchmarks are meaningless

Local models are always more accurate

The model is deliberately testing the user
Long conversations always corrupt a model's reasoning ability

questions.explanation: From the context-window module: the chat window scrolling back doesn't mean the model still has full access to everything in it. Suspect the context window before you suspect reasoning.
