title: Showing beats describing for format and tone
description: Why one worked example often does more than three paragraphs of description — and where the boundary of that advantage sits.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a worked example pins down format and tone more reliably than a description of them
Predict which of a described-only prompt or an example-based prompt produces more consistent formatting

contentSections.title: Description leaves room; an example doesn't

contentSections.body: A support lead wants ticket summaries in a specific internal shorthand: “CUST: [1-line issue] | SEV: [1-3] | NEXT: [owner + action].” She writes: “Summarize tickets in our internal shorthand format, it's pretty compact, includes severity and next steps.” The summaries that come back are compact-ish, sometimes include severity, rarely match the exact shape. She pastes in two real examples of the format instead — and the third ticket she runs matches it exactly.

contentSections.question: Why did pasting two real examples work so much better than describing the format in words?
contentSections.answer: A description like “compact,” “includes severity,” “next steps” leaves the exact punctuation, field order, and abbreviation style open to interpretation. An example shows the exact shape — the pipe characters, the field labels, the bracket style — with nothing left to guess.
contentSections.hint: Think about how many different formats could honestly be called 'compact' and 'includes severity and next steps' — versus how many formats match a specific example character-for-character.

contentSections.body:
A description of a format is a category; an example is a specific instance. “Compact, includes severity and next steps” describes an enormous space of possible formats that would all technically qualify — bullet points, a table, a one-line summary with commas, the exact pipe-delimited shorthand she actually wanted. The model has to pick one, and it usually picks whatever's most common in its training data for “compact ticket summary,” which is not the same as her team's specific internal convention.

A worked example collapses that space to one point. There's no ambiguity left about where the pipes go, whether severity is a number or a word, or whether “next steps” means a sentence or a name-plus-verb. This is the same specificity principle from the previous module, applied to something words are specifically bad at conveying precisely: exact visual and structural shape. Some things are much easier to show than to describe — and format is usually one of them.

contentSections.scenario: A writer wants blog post titles in a specific style — punchy, under 8 words, always starting with a number or a question. She tries describing this ('punchy, short, number or question') with mixed results, then pastes three titles she's happy with as examples.
contentSections.question: What's the model actually learning from the three pasted examples that the description didn't convey?

options.label: The specific pattern across the examples — word count, structure, opening style — inferred from real instances rather than named abstractly
The exact topics of those three posts, which it will now always write about
Nothing new — three examples and one description convey identical information

feedback.pattern-inferred: Right — the model generalizes a pattern from concrete instances, the same way a person shown three examples of a style starts to notice what they have in common, often catching details ('always starts with a number or a question') that a description might not think to spell out.
feedback.topics-only: The point of examples for style/format isn't to lock in the subject matter — it's to show the shape. A well-chosen example set should vary in topic while staying consistent in the thing you actually want copied: structure, length, tone.
feedback.no-difference: If they conveyed identical information, the described-only version wouldn't have produced worse results. The examples carry structural detail a short description leaves underspecified.

contentSections.concept: Examples let the model infer a pattern instead of guessing at an abstract description

contentSections.body: Some things are much easier to show than to describe — exact format and tone are usually two of them.

contentSections.title: Where description is actually fine

contentSections.body: Not every task benefits from an example. “Translate this paragraph into Spanish” doesn't need a worked translation example attached — the task is precise enough as a plain instruction that an example wouldn't remove any real ambiguity, just add length.

contentSections.code: A prompt for a task that already has one unambiguous correct shape (e.g. "convert this list of numbers to a comma-separated string") gets three worked examples of comma-separated strings attached, doubling the prompt's length.
contentSections.question: What's the flaw here?

options.label: The task was already unambiguous without an example — the examples add length without removing any real uncertainty
Examples always help regardless of the task, so there's no flaw
Three examples is too few — it needs at least ten to work

feedback.unneeded: Right — “comma-separated string” has essentially one reasonable interpretation already. Examples earn their cost by removing genuine ambiguity; when there isn't any, they're just extra tokens.
feedback.no-flaw: Examples aren't free — they cost prompt length and, for large example sets, processing time. When a task is already precise, that cost buys nothing.
feedback.too-few: The problem isn't quantity, it's that the task didn't need any examples at all — more of an unnecessary thing doesn't fix the unnecessariness.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Examples are a tool for closing a specific kind of gap: ambiguity about format, tone, or pattern that plain description leaves open. A task like 'comma-separate this list' doesn't have that kind of gap — description alone is already precise, so examples add cost without adding clarity.

contentSections.body: Reach for an example when a description would leave real ambiguity — not as a default add-on to every prompt.

title: Choosing examples that cover the edges
description: An example set that only shows the easy, typical case teaches the model the easy, typical case — and nothing about what to do with the messy ones.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when an example set fails to cover the edge cases a task will actually encounter
Select examples for a task that include at least one boundary or ambiguous case

contentSections.title: Three easy examples, one hard reality

contentSections.body: A prompt classifies customer messages as “complaint,” “question,” or “praise,” with three examples — one clean complaint, one clean question, one clean praise, each a single obvious sentence. In production, it handles clean single-topic messages fine and falls apart on “Thanks for the quick shipping, but the color was wrong” — a message that's genuinely both praise and a complaint, and the model picks one arbitrarily instead of flagging the mix.

contentSections.scenario: All three of the classifier's examples were clean, single-category messages. The model performs well on clean messages and unpredictably on mixed or ambiguous ones.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely mechanism?

options.label: The example set only demonstrated the easy case, so the model has no shown pattern for what to do with a message that doesn't cleanly fit one category
The model can only handle three categories total, and mixed messages exceed that limit
Mixed-sentiment messages are outside the model's training data entirely

feedback.no-edge-coverage: Right — examples teach by demonstration. If every demonstrated case is clean and unambiguous, the model has no shown precedent for messy cases, and it has to improvise — often by forcing a mixed message into whichever single category feels closest, since that's the only pattern it's seen.
feedback.category-limit: There's no such hard limit — the categories themselves aren't the issue; it's that a mixed *message* wasn't demonstrated at all, in any category.
feedback.outside-training: Mixed-sentiment text is common and certainly present in general training data — the issue is specific to this prompt's example set, not the model's underlying training.

contentSections.mechanism: An example set that only shows the typical case teaches the typical case, and leaves edge cases undemonstrated

contentSections.body:
A representative example set has to include the boundary cases the task will actually run into, not just three clean illustrations of the categories. For a classifier, that means at least one message that's genuinely ambiguous or spans two categories — plus a demonstrated way of handling it, whether that's picking the dominant sentiment, flagging it as mixed, or something else you've decided on. If the example set never shows a hard case, the model has nothing to generalize from when a hard case arrives, and it improvises in whatever direction the surrounding pattern nudges it — usually by force-fitting the message into one category rather than surfacing the ambiguity.

This matters most exactly where you'd expect: classification, extraction, and anything with defined categories or a fixed structure. The edge cases aren't rare exceptions to design around later — they're usually where most of the real errors in production actually happen, because the easy 80% was never going to need much help in the first place.
An example set that skips the hard cases teaches the model to be confident about the easy 80% and silent about the hard 20% — which is exactly backwards.

contentSections.title: What 'covering the edges' looks like in practice

contentSections.body: A recipe app wants a model to extract ingredient quantities into a structured list from user-submitted recipes. The examples given are all clean — “2 cups flour,” “1 tsp salt.” Real submissions include “a pinch of salt,” “flour, as much as it takes,” and “2-3 cloves garlic.” None of those get extracted sensibly, because nothing in the examples showed what to do with a vague or ranged quantity.

contentSections.scenario: Choosing examples to add to the recipe-extraction prompt.
contentSections.question: Which of these additions would actually improve edge-case coverage (versus just adding more of the same easy case)?

items.label: An example showing how to handle “a pinch of salt” (e.g. extracting it as quantity: 'to taste', not a number)
An example showing how to handle “2-3 cloves garlic” (e.g. extracting a range rather than forcing one number)
A fourth example of “3 tbsp olive oil” — another clean, single-number quantity
An example showing how to handle an ingredient listed with no quantity at all, like “salt and pepper”

explanation.vague-qty: This demonstrates a real pattern the clean examples never showed — a non-numeric, descriptive quantity — and gives the model a precedent for handling it consistently instead of guessing.
explanation.range-qty: Ranges are common in real recipes and structurally different from a single number; without a demonstrated example, the model has to decide arbitrarily whether to average, pick one end, or reject the range.
explanation.another-clean: This is the case that's already well-covered — adding a fourth similar example spends your example budget on the part of the task that was never the problem.
explanation.missing-qty: This is a genuinely different shape (no quantity field at all), and real recipes will absolutely include ingredients listed this way — worth one demonstrated example of how to represent an absence.

contentSections.synthesis: A good edge-case audit asks: what does a *real* input distribution actually contain, beyond the clean textbook case? Vague quantities, ranges, and missing fields are all things this task will genuinely encounter — each deserves at least one example. A fourth clean example doesn't buy anything the first three didn't already cover.

contentSections.body: Before finalizing an example set, ask: what messy, real version of this input have I not shown yet? That's usually where the errors will come from.

title: How many examples, and when more stops helping
description: Going from zero to one example is the single biggest jump. Going from five to fifteen usually buys almost nothing — and sometimes costs you.

learningObjectives.text: Predict the shape of the improvement curve as examples are added to a prompt
Identify signs that an example set has grown past the point of usefully helping

contentSections.title: The curve, not a straight line

contentSections.body: A team building a tone-matching prompt for customer replies starts with zero examples (bad, inconsistent tone), adds one strong example (big jump — noticeably more consistent), adds two more (smaller but real jump), and then, encouraged, adds twelve more, bringing the total to fifteen. Consistency barely moves from where it was at four examples — and the prompt is now long enough that it's slower and costs more per call.

contentSections.scenario: Same team measured tone-consistency (rated 1-10 by a reviewer blind to which prompt version they were scoring) at 0, 1, 3, 5, and 15 examples.
contentSections.question: Roughly what score, out of 10, would you expect at 5 examples versus at 15 — how many points of difference between them?
contentSections.explanation: In cases like this, the gap between 5 and 15 examples is often small — around a point or less on a 10-point scale — while the gap between 0 and 1, or 0 and 3, is usually much larger. The pattern isn't a straight line where each additional example buys the same amount of improvement; it's a curve that rises steeply at first and flattens once the pattern is already clearly demonstrated. Past that flattening point, more examples mostly add length and cost, not reliability.

contentSections.body:
Going from zero examples to one is usually the largest single jump you'll get — it's the difference between the model guessing at a format or tone from a description alone, and having one concrete instance to generalize from. A second and third example, especially if they show a genuinely different angle on the same pattern (different topic, same structure), usually buy real additional consistency, particularly for edge-case coverage. Past roughly four to six well-chosen examples, for most tasks, the marginal value of another example drops off sharply — the pattern is already clearly demonstrated, and a seventh clean example of the same thing you've already shown three times isn't teaching the model anything new.

This has a practical cost, not just a diminishing-returns curve: every example is tokens, and tokens are money and latency on every single call. A quality classifier that runs on every incoming support ticket pays the example-set cost thousands of times a day. Padding an example set past the point where it's actually improving output isn't neutral — it's a standing cost with no return.

contentSections.question: Put these five points on an example-count curve in order from smallest marginal improvement to largest marginal improvement (i.e., which added example bought the most extra consistency).
steps: Going from 8 examples to 15 examples (mostly redundant with the first 5-6)
Going from 5 examples to 8 examples (a modest, mostly edge-case gain)
Going from 3 examples to 5 examples (still adding real but smaller value)
Going from 1 example to 3 examples (a solid jump, especially for edge-case coverage)
Going from 0 examples to 1 example (the single largest jump)
contentSections.explanation: This mirrors a typical diminishing-returns curve: the first example does the most work by giving the model any concrete pattern to generalize from at all, each subsequent example (especially ones that add a genuinely new angle, like an edge case) buys real but shrinking value, and past roughly 5-8 well-chosen examples the returns are close to flat — extra examples mostly repeat a pattern that's already clearly established.

contentSections.body: The first example is worth the most. Somewhere around five to eight well-chosen ones, you're usually paying tokens for a pattern the model already has.

contentSections.title: When more examples actively hurts

contentSections.body: A prompt for generating product taglines includes fifteen examples, all pulled from the same one campaign, all with a slightly manic, exclamation-point-heavy tone the brand actually wants retired. New taglines keep coming back in that same tired voice, even after the instructions explicitly ask for something calmer — the sheer volume of same-toned examples is outweighing the explicit instruction.

contentSections.scenario: Fifteen same-toned examples versus an explicit instruction asking for a different tone. The examples win.
contentSections.question: What's happening here, mechanically?

options.label: A large, consistent block of examples is a strong repeated pattern in the context, and it can outweigh a shorter, one-time instruction that conflicts with it
The model ignores instructions entirely whenever any examples are present
Fifteen examples exceeds a hard technical limit, causing the prompt to malfunction

feedback.examples-outweigh: Right — there's no rule that instructions always beat examples or vice versa; both are just tokens in the context shaping the prediction. A large, uniform block of same-patterned examples is a strong, repeated signal, and it can outweigh a shorter, conflicting instruction, especially when the examples all agree with each other and the instruction stands alone.
feedback.ignores-instructions: Instructions aren't ignored categorically — plenty of prompts with examples also follow their instructions fine. The specific failure here is a *conflict* between a strong repeated pattern and a contradicting instruction, not a blanket rule about examples beating instructions.
feedback.hard-limit: There's no hard technical ceiling being hit at fifteen examples in a case like this — the issue is the content and consistency of those examples working against the stated instruction, not a count limit.

contentSections.concept: A large, uniform example set is a strong pattern that can outweigh a shorter, conflicting instruction

contentSections.body: This is the sharpest version of “more examples isn't free”: when an example set is both large and internally consistent, it functions as a strong statistical signal — stronger, in practice, than a short instruction that contradicts it. If you're deliberately trying to shift away from a pattern (a retired brand voice, an old format you're replacing), a big pile of old-pattern examples actively works against that shift, even paired with an instruction that says otherwise. The fix isn't more instructions insisting on the change — it's curating the example set itself: fewer examples, chosen specifically to demonstrate the *new* pattern, not the old one you're trying to leave behind.
Examples aren't background scenery an instruction can override — a large, consistent example set is itself a strong pattern, and it can win against a short instruction that disagrees with it.

title: Examples that accidentally teach the wrong pattern
description: An example set can be internally consistent and still teach something you didn't mean to teach — a coincidental pattern the model latches onto instead of the one you intended.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a coincidental, unintended pattern shared across an example set
Revise an example set to remove an accidental pattern while preserving the intended one

contentSections.title: The pattern you didn't mean to teach

contentSections.body: A prompt teaches a model to write encouraging feedback on student essays, with three examples — all three happen to be essays about environmental topics, because that's what was on hand when the examples were written. The model's feedback on a history essay keeps steering, unprompted, toward environmental connections that aren't relevant, because 'connect to environmental themes' is an accidental pattern all three examples shared.

contentSections.scenario: All three examples happened to be about the same topic, though topic was never the intended pattern to teach — tone and structure of encouraging feedback was.
contentSections.question: Why did the model pick up the coincidental topic pattern instead of just the intended tone/structure pattern?

options.label: The model has no way to know which shared feature across the examples was the intentional lesson and which was coincidental — it generalizes from whatever's consistently present
The model deliberately prefers environmental topics
Three examples is too few for tone to be learned at all, so topic was the only thing left to learn

feedback.cant-distinguish: Right — nothing in the examples themselves flags 'this part is the point, this part is incidental.' Every consistent feature across the example set is, from the model's side, an equally plausible candidate pattern to generalize from — topic included, whether or not you meant it to be.
feedback.prefers-topic: There's no preference for environmental topics specifically — the same failure would happen with any coincidentally shared topic across an example set, since the mechanism is generalizing from whatever's consistently present, not favoring a subject.
feedback.too-few-for-tone: Tone and structure genuinely were picked up too (the feedback is encouraging) — the issue isn't that tone failed to transfer, it's that an unintended pattern transferred alongside it.

contentSections.mechanism: The model generalizes from every consistent feature across an example set, not just the one you intended

contentSections.body:
Every example set has more than one consistent feature in it, whether you notice them or not — topic, sentence length, which pronoun shows up, whether every example happens to end on a positive note, whether every sample text is roughly the same length. The model has no way to separate “the feature I meant to teach” from “the feature that happened to be true of every example I picked.” It generalizes from all of them, and an accidental pattern that's coincidentally consistent across your examples is just as available to latch onto as the real one.

The practical defense is to vary everything you *don't* intend to teach, across your example set, while keeping consistent only the thing you do. If tone is the lesson, vary the topic across examples. If format is the lesson, vary the subject matter and the length of the input. Consistency in the intended pattern plus variation in everything else is what makes the intended pattern the only thing left that's reliably shared — everything else becomes noise the model can't build a false pattern from.
Whatever stays the same across every example, intentional or not, is a candidate pattern the model might learn — vary everything except the thing you actually want taught.

contentSections.title: Auditing an example set for hidden patterns

contentSections.body: Before shipping the essay-feedback prompt, a colleague reviews the three examples and asks a simple question: 'besides tone, what else is identical across all three?' The answer: topic (environmental), length (all around 400 words), and grade level (all high school). Each of those is a candidate for an accidental pattern.

contentSections.scenario: Auditing the three feedback examples for what's coincidentally consistent besides the intended lesson (encouraging tone and feedback structure).
contentSections.question: Which of these should actually be varied across a revised example set, to avoid teaching them as unintended rules?

items.label: Essay topic (all three were environmental)
Essay length (all three were around 400 words)
Assumed grade level of the writer (all three were high-school-level writing)
The feedback structure itself — one strength, one area to grow, one specific suggestion

explanation.topic: Topic should vary — otherwise 'connect to environmental themes' is a real risk, as seen in this lesson's hook.
explanation.length: If every example essay is the same length, the model might implicitly learn to expect or favor that length, which could bias how it treats notably shorter or longer real submissions.
explanation.grade-level: If every example is high-school level, the tone and vocabulary calibration might not transfer well to, say, a college essay or a middle-school one — varying grade level across examples, with the feedback register adjusted accordingly, would actually teach the intended adaptive skill better.
explanation.feedback-structure: This one *should* stay consistent — it's the actual intended pattern (one strength, one growth area, one suggestion), not an accident. Varying the thing you're trying to teach would defeat the purpose.

contentSections.synthesis: An audit like this separates 'what's the actual lesson' (feedback structure and encouraging tone — keep consistent) from 'what's just happened to be true of my examples' (topic, length, grade level — vary these deliberately so they don't get mistaken for the lesson).

contentSections.body: Before finalizing an example set, list everything that's consistent across it — then check each one: is this the actual lesson, or an accident of which examples I happened to grab?

title: Building a reusable example set
description: Turning a one-off good prompt into a saved, reusable example set that keeps working as the task and the inputs change.

learningObjectives.text: Build an example set for a recurring task that covers the typical case and its known edge cases
Design an example set that stays maintainable as new edge cases are discovered

contentSections.title: From one good run to something you can reuse

contentSections.body: A freelancer finally gets a prompt for tagging her invoices by project that works well — three good examples, covers the typical case and one edge case. Two months later, a new client structure breaks it, and she's back to editing examples ad hoc, in the same document, with no record of why each example was originally chosen.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways to store an example set: (A) three examples pasted directly into the prompt with no notes, versus (B) three examples each with a one-line note on what specific pattern or edge case it demonstrates, kept in a separate reference document she updates.
contentSections.question: Why does (B) hold up better over time?

options.label: When a new edge case appears, she can check what's already covered and add exactly what's missing, instead of guessing or duplicating
(B) produces better output on day one, regardless of maintenance
There's no real difference — both will perform identically

feedback.traceable: Right — the value of the notes shows up later, not on day one. When something breaks, a labeled example set lets you diagnose exactly what pattern is and isn't covered, instead of re-deriving that from scratch by staring at three unlabeled examples.
feedback.better-day-one: On day one, with the task and inputs fresh in mind, (A) and (B) can produce identical output — the labeling doesn't change what the model sees, only how maintainable the set is later.
feedback.no-difference: The difference isn't in immediate output quality — it's in maintainability. An unlabeled example set degrades into guesswork the moment the person maintaining it isn't the person who originally wrote it, or isn't remembering why.

contentSections.concept: A reusable example set needs to record why each example exists, not just what it contains

contentSections.body:
An example set built for a single good run and an example set built to be reused are different objects, even if they start out looking the same. The difference is documentation: for each example, a short note on what specific thing it's there to demonstrate — the typical case, this particular edge case, this specific format quirk. Without that note, a future edit (by you in two months, or someone else entirely) can't tell whether removing an example loses real coverage or just removes redundancy, and can't tell what kind of new example is actually needed when a new failure shows up.

The other habit worth building: keep the example set somewhere you'll actually find and update it, separate from a one-off chat, and treat a new production failure as a signal to add a labeled example for that specific case — not just to patch the individual bad output and move on. That's what turns 'a prompt that worked once' into 'a prompt that keeps working as reality keeps sending new cases at it.'
Label each example with what it's there to demonstrate — the label is what makes the set maintainable, not just usable.

contentSections.title: Building one from scratch

contentSections.body: Time to build one for real: a task you'd genuinely reuse a prompt for — categorizing something, extracting something, matching a specific format or tone repeatedly.

contentSections.intro: Build a reusable example set for: tagging incoming freelance inquiry emails as 'good fit,' 'not a fit,' or 'needs more info,' for someone who does this every week.

options: A clear inquiry with budget, timeline, and project scope stated — tagged 'good fit'
A one-word email that just says 'hi'
An email in a language other than English
fields.correctValue: A clear inquiry with budget, timeline, and project scope stated — tagged 'good fit'
fields.feedback: This is the bread-and-butter case the task will see most often — it belongs first, as the clear anchor example.

fields.prompt: Example 2 — a genuine edge case worth demonstrating
options: An inquiry with vague scope and no budget mentioned — tagged 'needs more info', with a note on what specifically triggers that tag versus 'good fit'
A second nearly-identical 'good fit' example
An email about an unrelated topic, like a newsletter signup confirmation
fields.correctValue: An inquiry with vague scope and no budget mentioned — tagged 'needs more info', with a note on what specifically triggers that tag versus 'good fit'
fields.feedback: This demonstrates the actual boundary between two categories — exactly the kind of case a clean example alone wouldn't teach.

options: An inquiry clearly outside the freelancer's actual services — tagged 'not a fit', with a note on the specific mismatch
A duplicate of example 1 with different names
An empty email with no text
fields.correctValue: An inquiry clearly outside the freelancer's actual services — tagged 'not a fit', with a note on the specific mismatch
fields.feedback: This covers the third category with an actual boundary case (clearly outside scope) rather than an implausibly obvious rejection, which is what the model will actually need to distinguish in practice.

fields.prompt: What should accompany each example in the saved reference document?
options: A one-line note on what specific pattern or edge case that example demonstrates
Nothing — the examples should speak for themselves
The exact date the example was written
fields.correctValue: A one-line note on what specific pattern or edge case that example demonstrates
fields.feedback: The label is what makes the set maintainable months later, when a new inquiry type shows up and you need to know what's already covered.

contentSections.synthesis: A reusable set for this task: one clean 'good fit' example as the anchor, one 'needs more info' example demonstrating the vague-scope boundary, one 'not a fit' example demonstrating the out-of-scope boundary — each labeled with what it's there to teach, stored somewhere she'll find it again, and treated as a living document she adds to the next time a real inquiry doesn't fit any of the three.

contentSections.body: A reusable example set covers the typical case plus the real boundaries between categories — and it's labeled well enough that updating it later doesn't require re-deriving why each example is there.

contentSections.title: Eight example-set judgment calls

contentSections.body: Eight quick scenarios about choosing, sizing, and auditing an example set — the same judgment calls that show up constantly once you're building prompts that need to run more than once.

title: Lab — Build an Example Set for a Classification Task
description: Build a real example set for a real classification or extraction task, measure accuracy before and after, and confront what changed.

learningObjectives.text: Build an example set covering the typical case and genuine edge cases for a real task
Measure and compare a task's accuracy before and after adding a worked example set

contentSections.title: A real classifier, measured before and after

contentSections.body: Pick a real classification or extraction task you could plausibly reuse — sorting emails, tagging notes, extracting fields from messy text, categorizing expenses. Something with real, if small, stakes to getting it wrong consistently.

contentSections.title: An example set, plus before-and-after accuracy
contentSections.brief: Choose a real classification or extraction task with at least 3 plausible categories or fields, and gather 10 real (or realistic) test cases you can run the prompt against — including at least 2-3 that are genuinely ambiguous or edge-case-y, not just clean textbook examples. First test a description-only prompt against all 10 and score it. Then build a labeled example set (typical case plus real edge cases) per this module, add it to the prompt, and re-run the same 10 test cases.
contentSections.deliverable: A description-only prompt and its accuracy on your 10 test cases, a labeled example set (each example with a one-line note on what it demonstrates), the example-augmented prompt, its accuracy on the same 10 test cases, and a short written conclusion naming which specific cases improved and why.

stages.title: Build the test set and baseline
stages.instructions: Gather 10 real or realistic inputs for your chosen task, including 2-3 genuinely ambiguous or edge-case ones. Write a plain description-only prompt (task, context, constraints, format — no examples) and run all 10 through it. Score each result right/wrong/partial against what you consider the correct output, and note the overall accuracy.
stages.checkpoint: You have 10 test cases, a description-only prompt, and a scored baseline result for each case.

stages.title: Build a labeled example set
stages.instructions: Following this module: pick one typical clean example and at least two genuine edge cases your test set actually surfaced (or that you know the real task encounters). Label each with a one-line note on what specific pattern it demonstrates. Audit the set for accidental shared patterns (topic, length, phrasing) that aren't the intended lesson, and vary those where you can.
stages.checkpoint: You have 3-5 labeled examples, each with a stated purpose, and you've checked for and addressed at least one accidental pattern.

stages.title: Re-test and compare
stages.instructions: Add the example set to your prompt and re-run the exact same 10 test cases. Score them the same way as the baseline. Compare case by case, not just the overall number — which specific cases flipped from wrong to right, and can you tie that to a specific example in your set?
stages.checkpoint: You have a second scored run on the same 10 cases, and a case-by-case comparison against the baseline.

stages.title: Write the conclusion
stages.instructions: Write a short conclusion: overall accuracy before and after, which specific cases changed and why (tied to a specific example, not a vague 'it got better'), and whether any case got worse — if so, why, honestly.
stages.checkpoint: You have a written before/after comparison naming specific cases and tying each change to a specific cause.

rubric.criterion: The test set includes genuine edge cases, not just clean examples
rubric.meets: At least 2-3 of the 10 test cases are ones a real deployment would find genuinely ambiguous or hard, not softballs.

rubric.criterion: Both prompt versions were actually run against the same test set
rubric.meets: Baseline and example-augmented accuracy are both measured on the identical 10 cases, not different or cherry-picked sets.

rubric.criterion: The example set is labeled and covers a real edge case, not just the typical one
rubric.meets: At least one example demonstrates a genuine boundary or ambiguous case, with a one-line note on what it's teaching.

rubric.criterion: The example set was checked for accidental patterns
rubric.meets: At least one potential accidental pattern (topic, length, phrasing) was identified and addressed by varying it across examples.

rubric.criterion: The comparison is case-by-case, not just a headline number
rubric.meets: The write-up names specific cases that changed and ties each to a specific example, not just an aggregate percentage.

rubric.criterion: Any regression is reported honestly
rubric.meets: If any case got worse after adding examples, that's named and explained rather than omitted.

contentSections.body: The number that matters isn't 'did accuracy go up' — it's 'which specific case improved, and can I point to the exact example that taught it.'

questions.prompt: A classifier's three examples are all clean, single-category messages. What's the predictable failure mode?

options.label: It handles clean cases well and improvises unpredictably on genuinely ambiguous or mixed cases it was never shown
It refuses to classify anything with fewer than five examples present
It performs identically regardless of example difficulty

questions.explanation: An example set that only shows the typical case leaves the model with no demonstrated pattern for the messy, real cases — which is usually where most production errors happen.

questions.from: This module — Teaching by Example
questions.prompt: A prompt has fifteen examples, all in an old brand voice, plus an instruction asking for a new tone. The old tone keeps winning. Why?

options.label: A large, internally consistent block of examples is a strong repeated pattern that can outweigh a shorter, conflicting instruction
Fifteen examples exceeds a hard technical limit and breaks the prompt
Instructions are always ignored whenever any examples are present

questions.explanation: Examples and instructions are both just tokens in context — a large, uniform example set is a strong signal that can beat a short, contradicting instruction.

questions.from: This module — Teaching by Example
questions.prompt: Three feedback examples are all about environmental-topic essays, though topic was never the intended lesson. What's the risk?

options.label: The model may generalize the coincidental shared topic as part of the pattern, alongside the intended tone and structure
There's no risk — the model only learns the intended lesson, never coincidental features
The risk only applies if there are more than ten examples

questions.explanation: The model can't distinguish an intentional pattern from an accidental one — every consistent feature across the example set is a candidate for what gets generalized.

questions.from: Previous module — The Anatomy of a Prompt
questions.prompt: What are the four components of a well-built prompt?

options.label: Task, context, constraints, format
Persona, tone, length, greeting
Question, hint, answer, example

questions.explanation: Task (the action), context (facts the model can't guess), constraints (boundaries), and format (output shape).

questions.from: Previous module — The Anatomy of a Prompt
questions.prompt: Why can 'don't mention the outstanding bug' backfire and produce a reply that awkwardly hedges around the topic?

options.label: Naming the excluded topic still puts it in the context the model predicts from — there's no mechanism that reliably erases it
The model deliberately disobeys instructions it disagrees with
Negative instructions specifically confuse the tokenizer

questions.explanation: Content-suppression negative instructions keep the topic live in context — stating the positive alternative usually works more reliably.

questions.from: Previous module — The Anatomy of a Prompt
questions.prompt: "You are the world's most brilliant marketing strategist, craft a stunning tagline." Why does this often produce a generic tagline?

options.label: The prompt is almost entirely persona and enthusiasm, with no actual facts about the specific product to differentiate it
The persona is too impressive and overwhelms the model
Taglines specifically can't be generated from role prompts

questions.explanation: An elaborate persona doesn't supply concrete facts about the actual product — specificity about the real thing is what was missing.

questions.from: Previous module — The Anatomy of a Prompt
questions.prompt: 'Explain this to a 4th grader' versus 'explain this to an AP Biology student' reliably produces two different-depth explanations. Why does this role framing work where a vague expert persona doesn't?

options.label: Audience is real, checkable information the model needs to choose vocabulary and depth — unlike a borrowed, informationless credential
It doesn't actually work any better — both are equally reliable
4th grade and AP Biology are specific certifications the model has memorized

questions.explanation: Audience framing supplies genuine information; an empty expert credential doesn't. That's the difference between a role prompt that helps and one that's theatre.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Where the Behaviour Comes From
questions.prompt: Why can't a single 'de-biasing' training pass fully remove bias from a model's outputs?

options.label: Bias enters at multiple independent stages (corpus, fine-tuning data, rater pool) that a later pass doesn't reach or reverse
Bias can't be reduced at all, at any stage
A de-biasing pass makes bias worse, always

questions.explanation: From the training module: a later pass can genuinely reduce specific patterns, but it's a patch on top of earlier stages it doesn't reach — it isn't a return to some bias-free default.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — The Settings That Change the Output
questions.prompt: What does raising a model's temperature setting actually change?

options.label: How strictly the model's own probability estimates are respected when sampling the next token — not what it 'thinks' is likely
How much the model 'cares' about getting the answer right
How many tokens of context the model can see

questions.explanation: From the settings module: temperature changes sampling strictness, not the underlying probability estimates themselves.

contentSections.body: A checkpoint that surfaces a wrong answer isn't a failure — it's telling you exactly what to re-read before the next module builds on it.

title: Asking for a shape, not just content
description: The difference between asking for the right information and asking for it in a shape you can actually use without reformatting it by hand.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a content request from a shape request
Predict which of two prompts produces output that can be used without manual reformatting

contentSections.title: Right content, wrong shape

contentSections.body: A researcher asks a model to “list the pros and cons of remote work.” She gets a genuinely good, accurate answer — four solid paragraphs, pros woven in with cons, some overlap between them. It's correct. It's also going to take her ten minutes to manually split into the two-column comparison table her report actually needs.

contentSections.question: The content was accurate and complete. What, specifically, cost her the ten minutes of rework?
contentSections.answer: She never told the model what shape the answer needed to take — a two-column table, pros and cons kept strictly separate. She only specified the content (pros and cons of remote work), so the model defaulted to prose, which is the typical shape for 'list the pros and cons of X' in ordinary writing.
contentSections.hint: The information itself wasn't wrong or missing — everything she needed was probably in there somewhere. What made it unusable as-is?

contentSections.body:
A prompt can nail the content and completely miss the shape, and the two are genuinely separate things to specify. “List the pros and cons” asks for content — which facts to include — but says nothing about structure: whether pros and cons should be interleaved in prose or split into two distinct columns, whether each point should be one word or a full sentence, whether there should be exactly four of each or as many as apply. Left unspecified, the model defaults to whatever shape is statistically typical for that kind of request, which for “pros and cons” is usually flowing prose — genuinely useful to read, genuinely annoying to extract structured data from.

This matters most exactly where the output needs to go somewhere else afterward: into a spreadsheet, a table, a form, another program. If you're going to have to reformat the answer by hand regardless of how good the content is, the prompt didn't actually save you the time it was supposed to — it just moved the work from 'writing' to 'reformatting.'

contentSections.scenario: Two prompts asking for the same underlying comparison. (A) “Compare Python and JavaScript for a beginner.” (B) “Compare Python and JavaScript for a beginner. Return a table with columns: Aspect, Python, JavaScript. Rows: Learning curve, Job market, Use cases, Common first project.”
contentSections.question: What did B specify that A left to the model's default?

options.label: The exact structure — a table, with named columns and named rows — instead of leaving the shape of the comparison undefined
B asked a harder question, which is why it got a better answer
B is simply a longer prompt, and longer prompts always produce more organized output

feedback.structure-named: Right — both prompts ask for essentially the same comparison; B additionally names the exact table structure, which is the piece A left entirely to the model's default (which, for 'compare X and Y,' is usually prose).
feedback.harder-question: The underlying question is the same difficulty in both — B didn't ask for anything new, it specified the shape the same content should take.
feedback.just-longer: Length isn't the mechanism — a prompt could add fifty words of unrelated detail and still produce prose. It's the specific naming of columns and rows that produces a table.

contentSections.concept: Shape has to be specified separately from content — the model won't infer a table from a request for a comparison

contentSections.body: Good content in the wrong shape still means manual rework — ask for the shape as explicitly as you ask for the facts.

contentSections.title: Naming the shape you actually need

contentSections.body: A small nonprofit needs a weekly volunteer sign-up summary that gets pasted straight into a shared spreadsheet: name, hours, task, in that column order, one row per volunteer. The first draft prompt just says “summarize who signed up this week” and produces a friendly paragraph naming everyone — accurate, unusable in a spreadsheet without being rebuilt by hand.

contentSections.code: "Summarize who signed up to volunteer this week and what they'll be doing."
contentSections.question: This produces an accurate paragraph that still has to be manually rebuilt into spreadsheet rows. What's missing?

options.label: An explicit structure: name the exact columns, the row-per-volunteer shape, and that it should be pasteable, not narrative
More volunteer details, like their contact information
A friendlier tone, since this is for a nonprofit

feedback.explicit-structure: Right — the content (who signed up, what they'll do) is already present and accurate. What's missing is any instruction about the output's literal shape — that it needs to be rows, with specific columns, not a paragraph.
feedback.more-details: Additional content wouldn't fix a shape problem — the paragraph could include every detail imaginable and still need manual restructuring into a table.
feedback.friendlier-tone: Tone isn't the issue here at all — a friendlier or blunter paragraph is still a paragraph, not a table.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix isn't more or different content — it's adding an explicit shape instruction: 'Return as a table: columns Name, Hours, Task. One row per volunteer, no extra text before or after the table.'

contentSections.body: If the output needs to go straight into something else — a spreadsheet, a form, another tool — say so explicitly. The model won't infer a destination it can't see.

title: Lists, tables and structured data
description: Choosing the right structure for the job — a flat list, a table, or key-value structured data — and specifying it precisely enough to get it consistently.

learningObjectives.text: Choose an appropriate output structure (list, table, key-value) for a given downstream use
Specify a table or structured-data request precisely enough to get consistent columns and fields

contentSections.title: Three shapes, three jobs

contentSections.body: A plain bulleted list, a table, and key-value structured data (like {"name": "...", "hours": 3}) look similar at a glance — all “structured” compared to a paragraph — but they're built for different downstream uses, and asking for the wrong one creates the same rework problem as asking for no structure at all.

contentSections.scenario: Someone needs to feed a model's output directly into a script that expects each record as a JSON object with fixed field names. They ask for “a bulleted list of each volunteer with their hours and task.”
contentSections.question: Why does a bulleted list, despite being 'structured' compared to prose, still fail here?

options.label: A bulleted list has consistent visual formatting but no guaranteed consistent field structure a script can parse — the script needs named, predictable fields, which is what key-value/JSON structure provides and a bullet list doesn't
Bulleted lists can't contain numbers
The model refuses to produce JSON unless explicitly told it's for a script

feedback.no-parseable-fields: Right — “Jane Doe, 3 hours, setup” as a bullet is readable to a person but has no guaranteed field boundaries a script can reliably split on, especially once a name has a comma in it or a task description varies in length. Key-value structure names each field explicitly, which is what a script actually needs to parse reliably.
feedback.no-numbers: Bulleted lists handle numbers fine — that's not the limitation here at all.
feedback.refuses-json: There's no refusal happening — the issue is that a bulleted list was requested, which is simply the wrong structure for a script's needs, not that JSON was forbidden.

contentSections.mechanism: Match the structure to the destination: prose for reading, a list for scanning, a table for comparing across items, key-value/JSON for a script to parse

contentSections.body:
A flat list is good for a person scanning a short set of items where order or grouping is the main information. A table is good when the same set of attributes needs comparing across many items — that's what columns are for. Key-value structured data (JSON-like objects, or a strict CSV with a fixed header row) is good when the output has to be read by another program, not a person, and that program needs to reliably find “the hours field” without guessing at commas or line breaks.

Picking the wrong one creates the same category of problem as asking for no structure: usable to a person, unusable to whatever comes next. And specifying “make it structured” without naming which structure just moves the guess from “should this be a list” down to “which kind of list” — the model still has to pick, and it'll pick based on what's typical for the request, not on what your downstream tool actually needs.
List, table, and key-value data aren't interchangeable synonyms for 'organized' — each is built for a different downstream use, and naming the wrong one still means rework.

contentSections.title: Getting consistent columns and fields

contentSections.body: A prompt asks for a table of five books with “title, author, and some details.” Run three times, the “some details” column comes back as genre once, a one-sentence summary the next, and publication year the third time — because “some details” never named a specific field, so the model picks a different plausible one each run.

contentSections.scenario: Fixing the book-table prompt for consistent columns across repeated runs.
contentSections.question: Which of these changes would actually produce consistent columns run after run?

items.label: Explicitly naming every column: 'Title, Author, Genre, Publication Year' instead of 'some details'
Including one filled-in example row showing the exact format expected
Adding 'please be consistent' to the prompt
Increasing the model's creativity/temperature setting, if available

explanation.name-columns: This directly removes the ambiguity — 'some details' was a vague placeholder the model had to interpret differently each time; naming the exact fields gives it nothing left to guess.
explanation.example-row: An example row (from the previous module's toolkit) shows the exact expected format concretely, reinforcing the named columns with a worked instance — especially useful if a field's expected format (like date style) still has room for variation.
explanation.ask-nicely: 'Please be consistent' isn't a checkable instruction — it doesn't specify what consistency means here (which columns, in what order), so it doesn't actually close the gap 'some details' left open.
explanation.raise-temp: Higher temperature increases variation in wording and sampling, which would make inconsistency worse, not better — the fix for a structural consistency problem is specificity, not a sampling setting.

contentSections.synthesis: Column drift almost always traces back to an underspecified field name. Naming every column explicitly — and pairing that with a worked example row when a field's format itself could still vary — is what produces the same shape run after run.

contentSections.body: If a column or field name is vague ('details,' 'notes,' 'info'), expect it to mean something different on every run — name every field explicitly.

title: Output you can paste straight into something else
description: The gap between output that looks structured and output that's actually pasteable — extra prose, inconsistent delimiters, and markdown that doesn't survive the trip into a plain-text field.

learningObjectives.text: Identify why structurally-correct-looking output still fails to paste cleanly into a destination tool
Specify a prompt so the output requires zero cleanup before pasting into a named destination

contentSections.title: Structured, and still unusable

contentSections.body: A prompt correctly produces a markdown table — clean columns, right data, right structure. It gets pasted into a plain-text CRM notes field that doesn't render markdown, and what shows up is a mess of pipe characters and dashes: “| Name | Hours |\n|---|---|\n| Jane | 3 |” — technically structured, completely unusable in its actual destination.

contentSections.scenario: The table's structure and content were both correct. The destination field renders plain text only, not markdown.
contentSections.question: What's the actual failure here?

options.label: The prompt specified structure (a table) but not the destination's actual rendering capability — markdown syntax that displays as a table in a chat window is literal pipe-and-dash characters in a plain-text field
The model made a formatting error and produced broken markdown
Tables can never be pasted anywhere outside of a markdown-rendering tool

feedback.wrong-syntax-for-destination: Right — the markdown was correctly formed; the mismatch is between markdown syntax (which needs a renderer to look like a table) and a plain-text destination (which just shows the raw characters). This is a destination-awareness gap, not a content or structure error.
feedback.broken-markdown: Nothing about the markdown itself is broken — pipes and dashes are exactly correct markdown table syntax. The problem is where it's being pasted, not how it was written.
feedback.never-pasteable: Tables in other formats — tab-separated values, comma-separated values, or plain aligned text — paste cleanly into plenty of plain-text destinations. Markdown specifically needs a renderer; it's not that tables in general can't be pasted anywhere.

contentSections.mechanism: A prompt has to specify the destination's actual capability (renders markdown? plain text only? needs tab-separated values for a spreadsheet paste?), not just 'give me a table'

contentSections.body:
“Give me a table” is a content and rough-structure request; it doesn't say what syntax the table should be written in, and different destinations need genuinely different syntax for the same underlying structure. Markdown tables render beautifully in a chat window or a markdown-aware editor and show up as raw pipe characters everywhere else. A spreadsheet paste usually wants tab-separated or comma-separated values, no markdown syntax at all. A plain-text field wants aligned columns using only spaces, or just accepts comma-separated data if that's what the workflow expects downstream.

The fix is naming the actual destination in the prompt, not just the abstract shape: “format as tab-separated values, ready to paste into a spreadsheet” or “plain text, comma-separated, no markdown formatting” tells the model which literal syntax to produce, instead of leaving it to default to whatever's most common for “a table” in its training data — which is usually markdown, because that's the common format in the technical and documentation text tables are heavily represented in.

contentSections.code: "Give me a table of these five expenses."
contentSections.question: This prompt is being used to generate data for pasting directly into a spreadsheet cell range. What's missing?

options.label: The actual required syntax for a spreadsheet paste — tab-separated or comma-separated values, explicitly, instead of leaving the model to default to markdown table syntax
The specific expense amounts, which weren't included
A request for the table to be color-coded

feedback.syntax-spec: Right — 'a table' without a named syntax defaults to markdown most of the time, which pastes as literal pipe characters into a spreadsheet rather than populating cells. Naming tab-separated or comma-separated values fixes it.
feedback.amounts-missing: The prompt is asking the model to organize five expenses presumably already provided elsewhere in context — the issue here is output syntax, not missing input content.
feedback.color-coding: Color-coding isn't relevant to whether the output pastes cleanly into cells — that's a decorative concern, not a structural one.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Fixed version: 'Give me these five expenses as tab-separated values — Date, Description, Amount — ready to paste directly into a spreadsheet, no markdown, no extra text.'

contentSections.body: 'A table' isn't one thing — it's markdown, TSV, CSV, or plain aligned text depending on where it's going. Name the destination, not just the shape.

contentSections.title: Stripping the narration around the data

contentSections.body: A prompt correctly produces tab-separated data in the right structure — but wraps it in “Sure! Here's your table of expenses:” before it and “Let me know if you'd like any changes!” after it. Both lines have to be deleted by hand before every single paste, forever, unless the prompt says not to include them.

contentSections.scenario: Adding 'Return only the data, no introduction, no closing remarks, no explanation' to a data-extraction prompt.
contentSections.question: Why does this specific instruction matter for pasteable output, beyond just tidiness?

options.label: Narration text breaks a direct paste into a structured field — every extra line has to be manually stripped before the data is usable, which defeats the purpose of automating the formatting in the first place
It makes the model respond faster
It's purely cosmetic and doesn't affect usability

feedback.breaks-paste: Right — a friendly opener and closer are genuinely pleasant in a chat conversation and genuinely disruptive when the whole point of the prompt is to paste the output directly somewhere else without editing it first.
feedback.faster-response: There's no established relationship between including this instruction and response speed — the effect is on output structure, not generation time.
feedback.cosmetic-only: It's not cosmetic when the whole workflow depends on a clean paste — narration text is exactly the kind of thing that has to be manually removed every single time otherwise, at real recurring cost.

contentSections.concept: Data meant for direct use needs an explicit 'no narration' instruction, or friendly wrapper text becomes a standing tax on every use

contentSections.body: Conversational wrapper text — greetings, summaries of what was done, offers to help further — is a genuinely reasonable default for a chat interface, where a person is reading the reply directly. It's dead weight the moment the output is meant to be piped straight into something else without a human reading it first. The fix is one explicit line: “output only the [table/list/data], nothing before or after it” — and it's worth testing that the instruction actually holds across a few runs, since it's exactly the kind of instruction that can quietly slip on a particularly chatty response.
If a human isn't going to read the reply before it gets used, say so — 'no narration, just the data' turns a chat reply into something pasteable.

title: Length control that actually works
description: Why 'keep it short' is unreliable, what actually constrains length, and how to get a genuinely predictable size.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why vague length instructions ('keep it brief') produce inconsistent results
Specify a length constraint that reliably produces output within a target range

contentSections.title: Why 'keep it short' isn't a number

contentSections.body: A prompt asks for “a brief summary” of a report. Run once, it's two sentences. Run again on a similar report, it's a full paragraph. Both are defensibly “brief” compared to the source report — “brief” just doesn't pin down a specific target the way a number does.

contentSections.question: Why does 'brief,' 'short,' or 'concise' produce such variable actual lengths, even though the model isn't being inconsistent on purpose?
contentSections.answer: Those words describe a relative, comparative quality — shorter than the alternative, not a fixed target. What counts as 'brief' can reasonably vary depending on the source material's own length and complexity, so the model's read of 'brief' shifts with the input, even though no rule was violated either time.
contentSections.hint: Is 'brief' a fixed target, or a description that depends on what it's being compared to?

contentSections.body:
Words like “brief,” “short,” “concise,” and “detailed” describe a relationship, not a number — brief *relative to what the topic could reasonably need*, which the model has to estimate freely each time, and that estimate reasonably shifts with how much source material there is or how complex the topic looks. Two runs producing different lengths isn't the model malfunctioning; it's the same word being interpreted sensibly against two different implicit baselines.

A number removes that ambiguity entirely: “in exactly 2 sentences,” “under 100 words,” “3-5 bullet points, each under 15 words.” Numbers are the one kind of length instruction that doesn't need to be interpreted relative to anything — they're a fixed target the model can actually check its own draft against as it goes, the same way a person redrafting toward a word count would.
'Brief' is relative and shifts with the input; a number is a fixed target — use the number when the length actually needs to be predictable.

contentSections.title: How tight the number actually is

contentSections.body: “Under 100 words” is usually respected closely. “Exactly 100 words” is a much harder target for a model to hit precisely — it's estimating length as it writes, not counting and revising the way a person drafting toward a strict count might. Knowing which kind of promise a length instruction can actually keep changes how you use it.

contentSections.scenario: A prompt asks for a product description in 'exactly 50 words.' The actual outputs, run 10 times, are checked with a word counter.
contentSections.question: Roughly what's the typical spread — how many words off from exactly 50 might a run land, even when the model is genuinely trying to hit the target?
contentSections.explanation: A spread of roughly plus-or-minus five to ten words around a stated exact target is common — the model is generating token by token and estimating length as it goes, not counting words and revising toward an exact count the way a person editing a draft would. An upper-bound instruction ('under 60 words') is much easier to reliably satisfy than an exact-count instruction ('exactly 50 words'), because it only has to stay under a ceiling, not land precisely on a number.

contentSections.body: Treat “exactly N words” as an aspiration, not a guarantee — useful as a rough target, unreliable as a hard constraint the way a spreadsheet formula would be. “Under N words” or a range (“between 40 and 60 words”) tends to hold up more reliably in practice, because it only requires staying on one side of a boundary rather than landing on an exact point. If a genuinely hard length limit matters — a character-limited form field, an API with a strict cap — the safer engineering move is validating and truncating or re-prompting programmatically after generation, rather than trusting a single prompt instruction to hit an exact number every time.

contentSections.code: A form field has a strict 160-character limit (like an SMS). The prompt says: "Write exactly 160 characters."
contentSections.question: What's the risk in relying on this instruction alone for a hard technical limit?

options.label: An exact-count length instruction is a rough target, not a guarantee — occasional overshoots would silently break a hard technical limit unless the actual output is validated afterward
160 characters is too short for a model to write coherently
There's no risk — exact character counts are always respected precisely

feedback.no-validation: Right — a length instruction is a strong nudge, not a guarantee, and a hard technical limit needs an actual check, not just a hopeful prompt. Occasional overshoot has to be caught before it breaks the field, not trusted away.
feedback.too-short: 160 characters is a perfectly normal length for models to write coherent text in — length itself isn't the issue.
feedback.no-risk: This is exactly the risky assumption the lesson is warning against — exact counts are approximate in practice, and a hard technical constraint needs real validation.

contentSections.flawExplanation: For a genuinely hard limit, the safer approach is generating with some margin ('under 150 characters' as a buffer) and validating the actual output length programmatically before it's used, rather than trusting a single exact-count instruction to hold every time.

contentSections.body: An upper bound holds up better than an exact count. For a genuinely hard limit, validate the actual output — don't trust the instruction alone.

title: Consistency across many runs
description: Getting the same structure back reliably across dozens or hundreds of calls — the difference between a prompt that works once and one that works as a pipeline.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific failure that breaks a structured-output prompt at scale even though it worked in testing
Design a structured-output prompt to fail predictably and visibly rather than silently, when it does fail

contentSections.title: It worked ten times. Then it ran a thousand.

contentSections.body: A prompt that extracts structured fields from customer feedback works perfectly across 10 manual test runs. Deployed to process a real backlog of 1,000 feedback entries, roughly 30 of them come back with a field missing, a slightly different key name, or an extra unrequested field — a 3% failure rate invisible in 10 tests, expensive at 1,000.

contentSections.scenario: 10 manual tests looked perfect. 1,000 automated runs revealed a consistent small failure rate.
contentSections.question: What does this gap between the small test and the large run actually tell you?

options.label: A small manual sample can look perfectly consistent while still having a real, low-single-digit failure rate that only becomes visible at volume — 10 successes don't prove 1,000 will all succeed
Something in the model broke specifically after the first few hundred runs
The 1,000-run version must have used a different, worse prompt

feedback.sample-too-small: Right — a 3% failure rate would show up in roughly 1 out of every 33 runs on average; 10 test runs have a real chance of missing it entirely by luck, which is exactly what happened here. Testing at meaningfully larger volume than 'a few manual checks' is what surfaces a rate like this before it costs something in production.
feedback.model-degrades: There's no mechanism by which a model's reliability degrades partway through an unrelated sequence of independent calls — each call is its own independent prediction, not part of a continuous session that could 'wear down.'
feedback.different-prompt: Nothing in the scenario suggests the prompt changed — the same prompt at small scale can genuinely look flawless while having a real failure rate that only surfaces with enough attempts to make it statistically visible.

contentSections.mechanism: A small manual test sample can hide a real failure rate that volume reveals — test at a scale that would actually catch it

contentSections.body: Ten manual test runs, all looking clean, tell you the prompt isn't obviously broken — they don't tell you it's reliable at scale. A 2-5% failure rate, which is common for structured-output prompts that haven't been specifically hardened, is close to invisible in ten spot checks and expensive at a thousand real runs, especially if nothing downstream is checking for it. If a prompt is going into a pipeline that will run it many times unattended, the testing has to happen at a volume that could actually surface a small but real failure rate — not just enough runs to feel confident.
A handful of clean manual tests proves a prompt isn't obviously broken. It doesn't prove the failure rate is zero — only running at real volume does that.

contentSections.title: Failing loud instead of failing quiet

contentSections.body: Of the 30 failed entries in the backlog run, most weren't blank or obviously broken — they had a plausible-looking but subtly wrong field, like a sentiment label spelled slightly differently ('Positive' instead of the expected 'positive'), which silently broke the downstream script's exact-match filter without throwing any visible error.

contentSections.scenario: Hardening the extraction prompt and the pipeline around it against silent structural failures.
contentSections.question: Which of these would actually help catch failures like this before they cause silent downstream damage?

items.label: Explicitly listing the exact allowed values for a field (e.g. 'sentiment must be exactly one of: positive, negative, neutral — lowercase') rather than describing it loosely
Validating each output programmatically against the expected schema before it's used downstream, and flagging mismatches instead of silently passing them through
Trusting that a well-written prompt won't need any downstream validation, since the prompt itself specifies the format
Manually spot-checking a larger sample (say, 50 instead of 10) before full deployment

explanation.exact-values: Naming the exact allowed values, case included, removes the specific ambiguity that caused 'Positive' versus 'positive' — the same specificity principle from earlier modules, applied to a fixed value set.
explanation.validate-after: This is the real safety net — no prompt, however well-written, is guaranteed to be perfect on every single run, so checking the actual output against the expected shape before it's used is what catches the cases the prompt itself didn't prevent.
explanation.trust-good-prompt: A well-specified prompt reduces the failure rate; it doesn't reduce it to zero. Treating prompt quality as a substitute for validation is exactly the assumption that let the 30 silent failures through undetected.
explanation.spot-check-more: A larger manual sample genuinely improves the odds of catching a low-single-digit failure rate before full deployment, though it's still a sample, not a guarantee — it's a real improvement over 10 checks, just not a substitute for downstream validation.

contentSections.synthesis: Two layers work together: tighter prompt specification (exact allowed values) reduces how often failures happen, and downstream validation catches the ones that happen anyway. Relying on prompt quality alone, with no check on the actual output, is what let a quiet field-name mismatch flow all the way through to break a script.

contentSections.body: A structured-output prompt going into a pipeline needs a validator behind it, not just a well-written prompt in front of it — something has to check the actual output, every time, not just trust it.

title: Practice — Specify Output Format for Eight Tasks
description: Eight drills on choosing structures, naming exact fields and destinations, controlling length, and catching silent structural failures. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Choose and specify an appropriate output structure for a given downstream use
