title: Lab — Build a Prompt Whose Output Feeds a Spreadsheet
description: Build a prompt that produces genuinely pasteable, structured output across ten real test runs — measured, not assumed.

learningObjectives.text: Build a prompt that produces consistently structured, pasteable output for a real spreadsheet destination
Evaluate a structured-output prompt's reliability across repeated runs against a stated schema

contentSections.title: Ten runs, checked against a schema

contentSections.body: Pick a real or realistic task that should produce spreadsheet-ready rows — extracting data from messages, logging something you track weekly, turning notes into a comparison table. Something with a genuine destination, not a hypothetical one.

contentSections.title: A prompt producing pasteable structured output across ten test runs
contentSections.brief: Choose a task whose output should paste directly into a spreadsheet as rows with a fixed set of columns. Build a prompt that names the exact columns, the exact syntax (tab- or comma-separated values, no markdown, no narration), and any fixed value sets a field should be restricted to. Run it against ten different real or realistic inputs, and check every single output against your stated schema — not just whether it looks plausible, but whether it would actually paste cleanly and parse correctly.
contentSections.deliverable: The prompt, the ten inputs used, the ten raw outputs, a schema-compliance check for each (pass/fail, with the specific failure noted for any that failed), and a short conclusion on the measured failure rate and what you'd change to reduce it.

stages.title: Define the schema and build the prompt
stages.instructions: Write down the exact schema first: column names, in order, the exact syntax (TSV/CSV, no markdown, no narration), and any field with a fixed set of allowed values (naming them explicitly). Then build the prompt around that schema, including an instruction to output only the data.
stages.checkpoint: You have a written schema (columns, syntax, allowed values) and a prompt built to produce exactly that shape.

stages.title: Run ten real inputs
stages.instructions: Gather ten different real or realistic inputs for your task — not ten variations of the same easy case, include a couple that are messier or more ambiguous than the typical one. Run each through the prompt in a fresh conversation and save the raw output for all ten, unedited.
stages.checkpoint: You have ten raw outputs from ten different real inputs, saved unedited.

stages.title: Check every output against the schema
stages.instructions: For each of the ten outputs, check it against your schema: right columns, right syntax, no narration text, any restricted-value fields using an allowed value. Mark each pass or fail, and for any failure, note exactly what was wrong — extra text, wrong column, unexpected value, wrong delimiter.
stages.checkpoint: You have a pass/fail result for all ten outputs, with specific failure reasons noted for any that failed.

rubric.criterion: The schema is fully specified before testing, not inferred afterward
rubric.meets: Column names, syntax, and any restricted value sets are written down before the ten runs, not reconstructed from looking at the outputs.

rubric.criterion: Ten genuinely different inputs were used, including some messier ones
rubric.meets: The ten inputs aren't ten near-identical easy cases — at least 2-3 are realistically messy or ambiguous.

rubric.criterion: Every output was actually checked against the schema, not just skimmed
rubric.meets: Each of the ten has an explicit pass/fail against the written schema, with specific failure reasons for any fails.

rubric.criterion: The output requires zero manual cleanup to paste, on a pass
rubric.meets: A passing output could be pasted directly into a spreadsheet's cell range with no editing — no markdown syntax, no narration, no extra text.

rubric.criterion: The conclusion states a real measured failure rate, not a vague impression
rubric.meets: The write-up states X out of 10 passed, names the actual failure modes seen, and proposes a specific fix for the most common one.

contentSections.body: A structured-output prompt isn't done when it looks right once — it's done when you've checked it against the schema enough times to know its real failure rate.

title: Checkpoint — Getting Output You Can Use
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Teaching by Example, two reaching further back to The Anatomy of a Prompt.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve output-structuring judgment calls from this module and the example-set judgment calls before it, without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Getting Output You Can Use

questions.from: This module — Getting Output You Can Use
questions.prompt: A prompt asks a model to 'list the pros and cons of remote work' and gets an accurate but prose-form answer that has to be manually split into a table. What went wrong?

options.label: Content was specified but shape wasn't — the model defaulted to prose, the typical shape for that kind of request
The model got the facts wrong, which caused the formatting issue
Pros-and-cons comparisons can never be returned as a table

questions.explanation: Content and shape are separate things to specify — leaving shape unstated means the model defaults to whatever's typical for the request, usually prose.

questions.from: This module — Getting Output You Can Use
questions.prompt: Someone asks a model for “a bulleted list” of records that then need to be parsed by a script expecting fixed JSON fields. Why does this fail?

options.label: A bulleted list has readable formatting but no guaranteed parseable field boundaries — key-value/JSON structure is what a script actually needs
Bulleted lists can't contain numeric data
Scripts can never parse model-generated output regardless of format

questions.explanation: Match the structure to the destination — a script needs named, predictable fields, which a bullet list doesn't reliably provide even though it's 'structured' in appearance.

questions.from: This module — Getting Output You Can Use
questions.prompt: A prompt correctly produces a markdown table, but it displays as raw pipe characters in a plain-text CRM field. What's the actual issue?

options.label: The prompt specified a shape (table) but not the destination's rendering capability — markdown syntax needs a renderer that this field doesn't have
The model produced broken markdown
Tables can never be used outside a markdown-rendering tool

questions.explanation: The markdown was correctly formed — the mismatch is between markdown syntax and a plain-text destination. Naming the destination's actual required syntax (TSV, CSV, plain aligned text) fixes it.

questions.from: This module — Getting Output You Can Use
questions.prompt: Why does 'exactly 50 words' tend to produce more variation in actual word count than 'under 60 words'?

options.label: An exact count requires landing precisely on a number while generating token by token, which is harder than just staying under a ceiling
'Under 60 words' and 'exactly 50 words' are functionally identical instructions
Exact word counts are always honored perfectly; the variation described doesn't actually happen

questions.explanation: Treat an exact-count instruction as a rough target, not a guarantee — an upper bound holds up more reliably because it only requires staying on one side of a boundary.

questions.from: Previous module — Teaching by Example
questions.prompt: Why does pasting two or three real worked examples of a format often outperform describing the format in words?

options.label: A description covers a whole category of possible formats; an example collapses that to one specific, unambiguous shape
Examples are always shorter than descriptions
Models can only follow instructions given as examples

questions.explanation: Description leaves genuine ambiguity about exact structure; an example removes it by showing the specific instance.

questions.from: Previous module — Teaching by Example
questions.prompt: A classifier's three examples are all clean, single-category messages. What's the predictable failure mode on a genuinely mixed message?

options.label: It has no demonstrated precedent for the mixed case and improvises, usually by force-fitting it into one category
It refuses to classify anything with fewer than five examples present
It performs identically regardless of example difficulty

questions.explanation: An example set that only shows the typical case leaves no shown pattern for the messy, real cases — usually where most production errors happen.

questions.from: Previous module — Teaching by Example
questions.prompt: Fifteen examples in an old brand voice keep winning over a short instruction asking for a new tone. Why?

options.label: A large, internally consistent block of examples is a strong repeated pattern that can outweigh a shorter, conflicting instruction
Fifteen examples exceeds a hard technical limit and breaks the prompt
Instructions are always ignored whenever any examples are present

questions.explanation: Examples and instructions are both just tokens in context — a large uniform example set is a strong signal that can beat a short, contradicting instruction.

questions.from: Previous module — Teaching by Example
questions.prompt: Three feedback examples are all about environmental-topic essays, though topic was never the intended lesson. What's the risk?

options.label: The model may generalize the coincidental shared topic alongside the intended tone and structure, since it can't distinguish intentional from accidental patterns
There's no risk — the model only learns the intended lesson
The risk only applies with more than ten examples

questions.explanation: Every consistently-shared feature across an example set, intentional or not, is a candidate for what gets generalized.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — The Anatomy of a Prompt
questions.prompt: What are the four components of a well-built prompt?

options.label: Task, context, constraints, format
Persona, tone, length, greeting
Question, hint, answer, example

questions.explanation: Task (the action), context (facts the model can't guess), constraints (boundaries), and format (output shape) — this module's format specificity builds directly on the fourth of these.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — The Anatomy of a Prompt
questions.prompt: Why does naming what NOT to discuss (e.g. 'don't mention the outstanding bug') sometimes backfire?

options.label: Naming the excluded topic still puts it in the context the model predicts from — there's no mechanism that reliably erases it
The model deliberately disobeys instructions it disagrees with
Negative instructions specifically confuse the tokenizer

questions.explanation: Content-suppression negative instructions keep the topic live in context — stating the positive alternative usually works more reliably.

contentSections.body: A checkpoint that surfaces a wrong answer isn't a failure — it's telling you exactly what to re-read before the next module builds on it.

title: Asking for steps and why it changes the answer
description: Asking a model to show its work doesn't just make wrong answers easier to catch — it often changes whether the answer is wrong in the first place.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why asking for intermediate steps can change a model's final answer, not just its transparency
Predict when a step-by-step request will meaningfully help versus add nothing but length

contentSections.title: The same question, two different answers

contentSections.body: “A store has 3 shelves. Each shelf holds 8 boxes, and each box has 12 items. A shipment removes 2 boxes from one shelf. How many items are left?” Asked directly, a model sometimes answers with the wrong number. Asked to “work through this step by step, showing each calculation before the final answer,” the same underlying model, on the same question, gets it right far more consistently.

contentSections.question: The question and the model didn't change. What did?
contentSections.answer: The model's own intermediate output became part of what it's predicting from. Asked to show steps, it first generates “3 shelves × 8 boxes = 24 boxes,” then “24 boxes × 12 items = 288 items,” then “2 boxes removed = 24 items removed,” each of which becomes context for the next step — instead of trying to jump straight from the question to a final number in one leap, with no intermediate scaffolding to build on or check against.
contentSections.hint: Remember the autoregressive mechanism: each generated token becomes part of the input for predicting the next one. What does 'show your steps' actually add to that input, mid-generation?

contentSections.body:
This isn't just a transparency feature — it changes the actual computation the model performs. Recall the core mechanism: every token a model generates becomes part of the context for predicting the next one. Asked for a direct final answer, the model has to get the whole multi-step calculation right in essentially one continuous prediction, with no intermediate result to build on or catch an error against. Asked to show steps, it generates “3 × 8 = 24” first, and that correct intermediate result is now sitting in the context, available to condition the next step on — “24 × 12 = 288” is now a prediction made with 24 already established as a token in front of it, not a number the model has to silently hold in its head through several more operations.

This is the practical reason “think step by step” reliably helps on multi-step problems: it isn't asking the model to reveal a hidden calculation it already did — there's no hidden calculation happening separately from what gets generated. Generating the steps *is* how the calculation gets done more reliably, because each step becomes real, checkable context for the next one instead of an invisible intermediate the model has to get right silently.

contentSections.problem: A bakery bakes 144 muffins. It sells them in boxes of 6, keeps 12 muffins aside for a display, and donates the rest of the boxes it can't fill completely. How many boxes get sold?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.work: 144 muffins total, minus 12 kept for display = 132 muffins available to box.
steps.why: The display muffins never enter the boxing process — subtracting them first avoids incorrectly boxing muffins that aren't actually available.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.why: This step only works cleanly because step 1 already removed the muffins that shouldn't be counted — doing the division on all 144 muffins first would silently bake in an error that's hard to spot in a single combined calculation.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.work: 132 ÷ 6 = 22 exactly, no remainder, so there are no leftover muffins that can't fill a complete box.
steps.why: Checking for a remainder is itself a step that only exists because the work was broken out — a single-leap answer has no equivalent moment to notice this.

faded.problem: A library has 250 books to shelve. It sets aside 10 for a special display, then shelves the rest in stacks of 8. How many complete stacks get shelved, and how many books are left over from the shelving (not counting the display ones)?

blanks.prompt: Step 1 — how many books are actually available to shelve, after the display set-aside?
blanks.why: Same pattern as the muffin problem — remove what's set aside before dividing, or the division silently includes books that were never going to be shelved.

blanks.prompt: Step 2 — how many complete stacks of 8 fit into that number?
blanks.why: This division is only correct because it's operating on the already-corrected 240, not the original 250.

blanks.prompt: Step 3 — is there a remainder, and if so, how many leftover books?
blanks.answer: 240 ÷ 8 = 30 exactly, so there are 0 leftover books
blanks.why: Checking explicitly for a remainder is a step a single-leap answer skips entirely, which is exactly where an off-by-a-few error tends to hide.

contentSections.procedure: Break the problem into the smallest steps where each one only depends on the result just before it — remove what shouldn't be counted, then operate on what's left, then explicitly check for a remainder or edge case rather than assuming a clean division.

contentSections.body: Asking for steps isn't just about seeing the work — generating the steps is how a multi-step answer gets computed more reliably in the first place.

contentSections.title: Where it adds nothing

contentSections.body: “What's the capital of Australia? Please think through this step by step.” The step-by-step request doesn't help here — there's no multi-step calculation to scaffold, just a single fact to retrieve, and the instruction mostly adds a few sentences of unnecessary padding before the same one-word answer.

contentSections.code: "What year did the Berlin Wall fall? Please reason through this step by step before answering."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in adding 'think step by step' to this specific prompt?

options.label: There's no multi-step calculation or reasoning chain here to scaffold — it's a single factual retrieval, so the instruction adds length without adding reliability
Step-by-step reasoning makes single-fact questions less accurate
The question is too easy for the model to answer at all

feedback.no-steps-needed: Right — step-by-step reasoning helps specifically when there's a real chain of intermediate results to build on. A single factual lookup like a well-known date doesn't have intermediate steps to generate context from — there's nothing for the mechanism from this lesson to actually help with.
feedback.makes-worse: There's no established mechanism by which asking for steps actively makes a single-fact answer less accurate — the more precise problem is that it doesn't help, not that it actively hurts.
feedback.too-easy: The instruction's cost isn't about difficulty — it's that a single-fact question has no multi-step structure for the technique to operate on, regardless of how easy or hard the fact itself is to recall.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Reserve step-by-step requests for genuinely multi-step tasks — arithmetic, multi-part logic, anything with intermediate results that build on each other. For a single fact, it's extra tokens and extra latency for the same underlying answer.

contentSections.body: Step-by-step reasoning earns its cost on genuinely multi-step problems. On a single-fact question, it's padding, not help.

title: Reasoning you can actually verify
description: Not all shown work is equally checkable — the difference between steps you could independently confirm and steps that just look thorough.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish reasoning that's independently verifiable from reasoning that merely looks detailed
Ask for reasoning in a form specifically designed to be checked

contentSections.title: Detailed isn't the same as checkable

contentSections.body: A model is asked to estimate whether a small business can afford a new hire, “showing its reasoning.” It produces four confident paragraphs about market conditions, growth trajectory, and industry benchmarks — detailed, well-organized, and containing zero actual numbers from the business in question, so there's nothing in it you could check against the business's real finances.

contentSections.scenario: The reasoning is long, well-structured, and confident, but contains no specific numbers, named assumptions, or a calculation someone could re-check independently.
contentSections.question: What's actually missing here, mechanically?

options.label: The reasoning is fluent prose about the topic, not a traceable chain of stated assumptions and calculations someone could independently verify or challenge
The reasoning is too long — shorter reasoning is always more verifiable
The model is deliberately hiding the real numbers

feedback.not-traceable: Right — 'showing reasoning' was interpreted as 'writing about the topic at length,' which is a fluent, confident-sounding continuation, but it's not the same as a chain of specific, checkable steps. There's no stated assumption to agree or disagree with, no number to verify, nothing to trace back to a source.
feedback.too-long: Length isn't the actual problem — a long explanation could still be fully traceable if it named specific figures and assumptions at each step. It's the absence of checkable content, not the word count, that's the issue.
feedback.deliberately-hiding: There's no concealment happening — the model produced exactly what a vague 'show your reasoning' request tends to produce: confident, on-topic prose, generated the same way any other text is, with no separate step that decided to withhold numbers.

contentSections.mechanism: A vague 'show your reasoning' request can produce fluent, confident, on-topic prose with nothing specific in it to actually check

contentSections.body:
There's a real difference between reasoning that's detailed and reasoning that's checkable. Detailed reasoning can still be entirely made of general, plausible-sounding statements — “market conditions suggest cautious optimism” — that have no specific claim in them a person could verify true or false. Checkable reasoning names its inputs explicitly: the actual revenue figure being used, the actual assumption being made (“assuming revenue stays flat for the next two quarters”), the actual calculation performed on those numbers. A person reading it can find the exact place they disagree, plug in a different number, and see how the conclusion changes.

The fix isn't asking for more reasoning — it's asking for a specific kind of reasoning: “state every number and assumption you're using explicitly, then show the calculation that follows from them.” That single instruction is the difference between reasoning you can audit and reasoning you can only either trust or ignore.
Ask what specifically you could check in a piece of reasoning. If the honest answer is 'nothing, it's just confident prose,' it isn't verifiable reasoning, whatever it looks like.

contentSections.title: Building in the check

contentSections.body: A prompt estimating a project's timeline is rewritten to require: “List every assumption as a labeled line before the estimate — e.g. 'Assumption: 2 developers, full-time.' Then show the calculation. Then state what would change the estimate if any one assumption were wrong.” The new version is genuinely arguable — a reader can pick the one assumption they disagree with and immediately see what it would do to the number.

contentSections.scenario: Comparing 'estimate the project timeline' to the rewritten version requiring labeled assumptions, a shown calculation, and a sensitivity note.
contentSections.question: What does the rewritten version actually add, mechanically?

options.label: It forces the model to make its inputs explicit as separate, checkable tokens in the output, rather than folding them invisibly into a single confident number
It makes the model calculate the timeline more accurately by trying harder
It guarantees the final number will be correct

feedback.explicit-inputs: Right — labeling each assumption as its own line is what makes it checkable at all. A bare final number has no separable pieces to agree or disagree with; a labeled-assumption version does, whether or not the final number itself turns out to be right.
feedback.tries-harder: There's no mechanism for a model to 'try harder' — the change is in what's asked for (explicit, separable inputs) not in effort applied to the same underlying task.
feedback.guarantees-correct: Making reasoning checkable doesn't make it correct — it makes an error, if there is one, findable. Those are different, both useful, properties.

contentSections.concept: Checkable reasoning surfaces its inputs as separate, labeled, arguable pieces instead of folding them into one confident number

contentSections.body: Verifiable reasoning isn't a guarantee of a correct answer — it's a guarantee that if the answer is wrong, you have a real shot at finding out where and why, instead of just distrusting the whole thing or trusting it blindly. That's the actual goal of asking for structured, labeled reasoning: not certainty, but auditability. A wrong number with its assumptions laid bare is more useful than a right number you can't check, because you can't tell those two apart from the outside without the assumptions being visible in the first place.
The goal of asking for verifiable reasoning isn't a guaranteed-correct answer — it's an answer where a wrong step, if there is one, can actually be found.

title: Plausible reasoning that reaches a wrong answer
description: Shown steps can look coherent, follow logically from each other, and still land on a wrong conclusion — because one step, usually early, was quietly wrong.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the point in a chain of reasoning where an error was introduced, given the full chain
Explain why fluent, well-structured reasoning doesn't guarantee a correct conclusion

contentSections.title: Every step follows. The answer is still wrong.

contentSections.body: A model reasons through a word problem: “A train travels 60 mph for 2 hours, covering 120 miles. It then travels 40 mph for 3 hours, covering another 120 miles. Total distance: 240 miles. Total time: 5 hours. Average speed: 240 ÷ 5 = 48 mph.” Every individual arithmetic step is correct. The final answer is also, in this case, actually correct — but change one detail and the same clean-looking reasoning style can carry a wrong number through to the end just as smoothly.

contentSections.scenario: A near-identical reasoning chain: '60 mph for 2 hours = 120 miles. 45 mph for 3 hours = 145 miles. Total distance: 265 miles. Total time: 5 hours. Average speed: 265 ÷ 5 = 53 mph.' (45 × 3 is actually 135, not 145 — a single early arithmetic slip.)
contentSections.question: Why does the final answer look just as confident and well-formed as a correct chain, despite the error?

options.label: Each later step correctly follows from the (wrong) number before it — the reasoning's internal consistency doesn't depend on any individual step's number being actually correct, only on later steps building coherently on whatever came before
The model knows the answer is wrong but presents it confidently anyway
Errors like this only happen in reasoning the model wasn't asked to show

feedback.consistent-not-correct: Right — 265 ÷ 5 = 53 is itself correct arithmetic, performed correctly on an already-wrong number. Internal consistency (each step following from the last) is a different property from correctness (each step being actually right), and fluent, well-structured reasoning only guarantees the first one.
feedback.knows-its-wrong: There's no separate awareness checking the work against ground truth — the model is generating each token as a likely continuation of what came before, including a plausible-looking but arithmetically wrong intermediate result, with the same fluency either way.
feedback.only-hidden: This exact failure mode happens in shown reasoning just as easily as hidden reasoning — showing the work makes an error like this findable, but doesn't prevent it from occurring in the first place.

contentSections.mechanism: Fluent internal consistency (each step follows from the last) is not the same guarantee as correctness (each step is actually right) — reasoning can have one without the other

contentSections.body:
This is the sharpest, most practically important limit of “ask it to show its reasoning”: showing the work makes an error *findable*, it doesn't make an error *impossible*. A single wrong intermediate value — a multiplication slip, a misread number, a wrong assumption stated early — can propagate cleanly through several subsequent steps that are each, individually, performed correctly on the number they were handed. The chain reads as coherent because it is coherent; each step really does follow from the one before it. What broke happened earlier, in a step that looked exactly as confident and well-formed as every other step around it.

This is exactly why verifiable reasoning (from the previous lesson) matters more than confident-looking reasoning: a chain with explicit, checkable intermediate values is one where you can actually go find the wrong step. A chain that's just fluent and well-organized, with the same wrong number folded in early, gives you nothing to check against — you'd have to redo the whole calculation yourself to catch it, which is exactly the work you were hoping the shown reasoning would save you.

A chain of reasoning can be internally consistent — every step correctly following the last — while still being wrong, because one early step was wrong and everything after it just correctly built on that mistake.

contentSections.title: Finding the broken link

contentSections.body: Given a full, plausible-looking reasoning chain that reaches a wrong conclusion, the practical skill isn't re-deriving the whole answer from scratch — it's checking each step against the one before it, specifically looking for the first place where the step doesn't actually follow, rather than reading the whole thing and judging it by its overall confident tone.

contentSections.question: A colleague hands you this reasoning chain and says the final answer feels off: '(1) A conference has 340 attendees. (2) 15% are students, so 340 × 0.15 = 61 students. (3) Students get a $20 discount off the $150 ticket, so they each pay $130. (4) Total revenue: 279 non-students × $150 + 61 students × $130 = $41,850 + $7,930 = $49,780.' Put these four verification actions in the order you'd actually do them to find the broken link efficiently.
steps: Check step 2's arithmetic first, since every later step depends on its output: 340 × 0.15 = 51, not 61
Recognize that step 3 and step 4 are following correctly from step 2's number, even though that number is wrong
Recompute step 4 using the corrected count (289 non-students, 51 students) rather than trusting the original total
Report the specific broken link (step 2's multiplication) rather than just noting the final total 'looks off'
contentSections.explanation: Working forward from the first dependency, not backward from the final number, is the efficient path: step 2 is the earliest calculation and everything downstream depends on it, so checking it first either clears it or finds the break immediately. Here it finds the break — 340 × 0.15 is 51, not 61 — and every step afterward (3 and 4) is legitimately consistent with that wrong number, which is exactly the trap from this lesson's first pod. The useful output isn't 'the total seems wrong,' it's naming the specific step where the chain actually broke.

contentSections.body: When a reasoning chain's answer looks off, check the earliest steps first — errors compound forward, and a late step is almost always innocently building on an earlier mistake, not the source of it.

title: Breaking one hard task into several easy ones
description: The same scaffolding effect that helps with a multi-step calculation works, deliberately, on tasks that are hard specifically because they bundle several distinct jobs into one request.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when a single hard-seeming task is actually several distinct sub-tasks bundled together
Decompose a bundled task into a sequence of prompts, each producing a checkable intermediate result

contentSections.title: One prompt, several jobs

contentSections.body: “Read this customer interview transcript, identify the three biggest pain points, and write a product brief addressing each one.” As a single prompt, the output is uneven — the pain-point identification is sometimes shallow, because it's competing for the same generation pass as drafting a whole product brief, and a shaky first step quietly weakens everything built on it.

contentSections.scenario: The single bundled prompt asks for extraction (find pain points), analysis (which three are biggest), and generation (write a brief) all in one pass, and the middle step — choosing the actual three biggest pain points — often gets the least genuinely careful treatment.
contentSections.question: Why does bundling three distinct jobs into one prompt tend to shortchange the middle one specifically?

options.label: Nothing forces the model to treat extraction, judgment, and generation as separate, deliberate stages — it's one continuous generation, and there's no natural pause to genuinely reconsider the pain-point selection before writing starts flowing into brief-drafting mode
The model can only handle two tasks in a single prompt
Product briefs are inherently harder to write than pain-point extraction

feedback.no-natural-pause: Right — a single combined prompt has no built-in moment where the model is forced to commit to and double check the pain-point selection before moving into drafting the brief around it. It's one continuous stream of generation, and a hasty middle judgment can just carry forward into confident-sounding prose built on top of it.
feedback.two-task-limit: There's no hard cap at two bundled tasks — the issue isn't a count limit, it's that bundling any number of genuinely distinct jobs into one pass removes the natural checkpoint between them.
feedback.briefs-harder: Difficulty of the individual tasks isn't the mechanism here — the problem is structural: no deliberate pause exists between the judgment step and the generation step, regardless of which one is intrinsically harder.

contentSections.mechanism: A bundled multi-job prompt has no natural pause between distinct jobs — splitting them into separate prompts creates that pause deliberately

contentSections.body:
This is the same underlying idea as step-by-step arithmetic, applied one level up: instead of asking a model to silently do extraction, judgment, and writing all in one breath, split them into separate prompts run in sequence, where each one produces a result you can actually look at before moving to the next. First prompt: “list every pain point mentioned in this transcript, quoting the relevant line for each.” Second prompt, using that list as input: “which three of these are the most significant, and why — rank them.” Third prompt, using the ranked three: “write a product brief addressing these three specifically.”

Each step becomes something you can check on its own terms — did it actually catch the real pain points, does the ranking make sense, does the brief actually address what was ranked — instead of one long output where a weak middle judgment is invisible, buried inside otherwise fluent, confident prose.
A prompt that's actually three jobs in a trenchcoat produces a shakier middle job than three separate prompts would — split it, and check each piece before building the next one on top of it.

contentSections.title: Deciding what's actually worth splitting

contentSections.body: Not every multi-part-sounding task benefits from being split. “Fix the typos in this paragraph and make sure it's formatted as a bulleted list” is two small, low-stakes, easily-verified-together actions — splitting it into two separate prompts would mostly just add friction, not reliability.

contentSections.scenario: Deciding which of these tasks genuinely benefit from being decomposed into separate, sequential prompts.
contentSections.question: Which of these are good candidates for splitting into multiple prompts, per this lesson's reasoning?

items.label: Extract pain points from a transcript, rank them, then write a brief around them
Fix typos in a paragraph and format it as a bulleted list
Audit a codebase for security issues, prioritize them by severity, then draft a remediation plan for the top three
Translate a sentence to French and make it slightly shorter

explanation.interview-brief: This genuinely bundles extraction, judgment, and generation — exactly the pattern where a shaky middle step (the ranking) gets buried inside fluent final prose. Splitting it creates a checkable intermediate at the judgment step.
explanation.typo-format: Both actions here are small, low-stakes, and easy to verify together in the final output at a glance — there's no meaningfully hard judgment step being buried by bundling them, so splitting mostly adds overhead without adding real reliability.
explanation.audit-recommend: This has the same structure as the interview-brief case: extraction (finding issues), judgment (prioritizing by severity, which is exactly the kind of step worth being able to check on its own), and generation (the remediation plan) — a strong candidate for splitting.
explanation.translate-shorten: Translation and a minor length trim are both simple enough to verify together by reading the one output — there's no hidden judgment call getting buried the way there is in the security-audit case.

contentSections.synthesis: The signal for 'split this' isn't 'does the prompt ask for more than one thing' — plenty of small multi-part requests are fine bundled. It's specifically whether there's a real judgment or extraction step in the middle that's hard to verify once it's buried inside a longer, fluent final output.

contentSections.body: Split a task when there's a real judgment call buried in the middle of it that you'd otherwise have no way to check. Don't split every multi-part-sounding request out of habit.

title: Asking it to check its own answer, and the limits of that
description: Self-review genuinely catches some errors and genuinely misses others — knowing which kind is which is what makes it a useful tool instead of a false sense of safety.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why asking a model to review its own answer catches some errors but not others
Design a self-review prompt more likely to catch a genuine error than to just re-confirm the original answer

contentSections.title: What self-review actually catches

contentSections.body: A model computes a multi-step total, then, asked to “double-check your work,” re-walks the same calculation and catches a genuine arithmetic slip from step 2 — the second pass generates the calculation fresh, and this time the multiplication comes out right, correcting the earlier answer.

contentSections.scenario: Asked to double-check a calculation, a model catches a genuine arithmetic error in its own earlier work.
contentSections.question: Why does this kind of self-review sometimes actually work?

options.label: A second, independent generation pass at the same calculation isn't guaranteed to repeat the exact same slip — the two passes aren't the same computation reused, they're two separate predictions, and one catching what the other missed is a real, if inconsistent, benefit
The model has a genuine memory of having made a mistake and consciously corrects it
Asking to double-check always produces a correct answer, since the model tries harder the second time

feedback.independent-pass: Right — there's no guarantee the exact same slip repeats on a second, separately-generated attempt at the same calculation, so a second pass genuinely has a real, if not reliable, chance of landing on the correct number where the first one didn't. That's a real benefit, distinct from any actual awareness of the earlier mistake.
feedback.genuine-memory: There's no persistent internal record being consulted — the second pass is a fresh generation, conditioned on the request to double-check and the earlier answer being present in context, not a recollection of having erred.
feedback.always-correct: Self-review measurably helps on some genuine slips; it doesn't reliably fix every error, and there's no mechanism guaranteeing a second attempt is always right — it's a probabilistic improvement, not a certainty.

contentSections.concept: Self-review works, when it works, because a second independent generation isn't guaranteed to repeat the first pass's specific mistake — not because the model is consciously correcting itself

contentSections.body: Self-review has a real, if limited, mechanism behind it: a second generation pass at the same problem is a separate prediction, not a replay of the first one, so it has a genuine chance of landing somewhere different — including somewhere more correct — especially for a mechanical slip like an arithmetic error that isn't rooted in a deeper misunderstanding. That's worth using. It's also worth being precise about what it is: not the model consciously catching its own mistake the way a person re-checking their work would, but a second independent attempt that sometimes, not always, differs from the first in a useful direction.
Self-review can catch a genuine slip because the second attempt is a separate prediction, not a guaranteed repeat of the first — that's a real but limited benefit, not conscious error-correction.

contentSections.title: What it reliably misses

contentSections.body: The same model, asked to fabricate a citation earlier in a conversation, is then asked “are you sure that citation is accurate? Double-check it.” It confidently reaffirms the fabricated citation as correct — because “double-checking” a fact the model never had reliable access to in the first place isn't a mechanism that can produce reliable access to it now.

contentSections.code: A workflow relies entirely on "ask the model to fact-check its own claim" as the verification step for any specific factual assertion it makes, with no external source consulted.
contentSections.question: What's the structural flaw in this as a verification strategy?

options.label: Self-review can catch mechanical slips within a self-contained calculation, but it has no access to external ground truth — asking it to verify a fact it fabricated just produces another prediction from the same ungrounded process, not an actual check against reality
Models refuse to fact-check their own claims
Self-review only works for questions phrased as a double-check, never a fact-check

feedback.no-ground-truth: Right — this is the boundary that matters: self-review can genuinely help with self-contained reasoning, where a second pass has a real independent shot at getting the internal logic right. It cannot supply external verification for a specific real-world fact, because the second pass has exactly the same lack of access to ground truth as the first one did — there's no new information introduced by asking again.
feedback.refuses: There's no refusal happening — the model readily 'double-checks' and often reaffirms the original claim confidently, which is precisely the risk, not a safety mechanism kicking in.
feedback.phrasing-issue: The specific wording of the double-check request isn't the limiting factor — the limitation is structural: no external source was consulted either time, regardless of how the request is phrased.

contentSections.flawExplanation: For a specific factual claim — an obscure statistic, a citation, a precise figure — real verification requires an actual external source, not another round of the same prediction process that produced the claim in the first place. Self-review is a tool for catching internal-logic slips, not a substitute for checking a fact against reality.

contentSections.body: Self-review can catch a slip inside a self-contained calculation. It can't manufacture access to a fact the model didn't reliably have — for that, only an external source actually checks anything.
