learningObjectives.text: Judge whether a task genuinely benefits from step-by-step reasoning or task decomposition
Locate the specific point of failure in a plausible but wrong reasoning chain

contentSections.title: Eight reasoning judgment calls

contentSections.body: Eight quick scenarios about when to ask for shown work, how to tell verifiable reasoning from confident prose, and where self-review actually helps.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Solve a Multi-Step Problem With Checkable Steps
description: Take on a genuinely multi-step real problem, get it solved with verifiable reasoning, and independently verify each step yourself before trusting the final answer.

learningObjectives.text: Prompt for verifiable, step-by-step reasoning on a genuine multi-step problem
Independently verify each intermediate step of a reasoning chain rather than trusting the final answer alone

contentSections.title: A real multi-step problem, checked step by step

contentSections.body: Pick a genuinely multi-step problem from your own life or work with a real, checkable right answer — a budget calculation, a schedule with several constraints, a unit-conversion-heavy estimate, a multi-part logic puzzle. Something where getting it wrong would actually cost you something, even if small.

contentSections.title: A worked solution where you verified each step independently
contentSections.brief: Choose a real problem with at least 3 distinct calculation or reasoning steps and one genuinely correct answer you can determine independently (by hand, with a calculator, or against a known fact). Prompt for a solution with explicit, labeled, checkable reasoning — every assumption and intermediate value stated. Then verify each individual step yourself, not just the final number, and document where (if anywhere) it broke.
contentSections.deliverable: The problem statement, the prompt used, the full reasoning chain produced, your independent verification of each individual step (not just the final answer), and a written note on whether the chain was correct, and if not, exactly which step broke and what the correct value should have been.

stages.title: Choose the problem and prompt for checkable reasoning
stages.instructions: Pick a real multi-step problem with a genuinely correct answer you can verify independently. Write a prompt that asks for every assumption and intermediate value to be stated explicitly and labeled, not folded into a single final number — per this module's lesson on verifiable reasoning.
stages.checkpoint: You have a problem with a genuine correct answer, and a full reasoning chain from the model with labeled, explicit intermediate steps.

stages.title: Verify every step independently, not just the final answer
stages.instructions: Go through the reasoning chain step by step, checking each individual calculation or claim against your own independent work — not by re-reading it and judging whether it feels right, but by actually recomputing or re-checking each step's specific number or claim.
stages.checkpoint: Every individual step in the chain has been independently checked, with a clear right/wrong mark, not just an overall impression of the final answer.

stages.title: Document what you found
stages.instructions: Write up whether the reasoning was fully correct. If it wasn't, name the exact step where it broke, what the correct value should have been, and whether later steps were internally consistent with the wrong value (the propagation pattern from this module's third lesson) or introduced further separate errors.
stages.checkpoint: You have a written verdict naming the specific step, if any, where the reasoning broke, distinct from a general 'the answer was right/wrong.'

rubric.criterion: The problem has a genuine, independently-checkable correct answer
rubric.meets: You could verify correctness without relying on the model's own claim — by hand-calculation, a known reference fact, or an independent tool.

rubric.criterion: The reasoning chain has explicit, labeled intermediate steps
rubric.meets: Every assumption and calculation is stated as a separate, identifiable step, not folded into prose or a single final number.

rubric.criterion: Every step was independently verified, not just the final answer
rubric.meets: Each individual step has its own recorded verification, not a single pass/fail judgment on the whole chain.

rubric.criterion: Any broken step is named specifically
rubric.meets: If the chain was wrong, the write-up names the exact step, not just 'the answer was off.'

rubric.criterion: The write-up distinguishes propagated errors from fresh errors
rubric.meets: If multiple steps were wrong, the write-up notes whether later wrong steps were correctly built on an earlier mistake (propagation) or were independently wrong on their own terms.

contentSections.body: Verifiable reasoning only pays off if you actually verify it — a labeled chain you don't check is just a longer version of trusting the final number.

title: Checkpoint — Making It Show Its Work
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Getting Output You Can Use, two reaching further back to The Anatomy of a Prompt.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the reasoning-prompting judgment calls from this module and the output-structuring judgment calls before it, without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Making It Show Its Work

questions.from: This module — Making It Show Its Work
questions.prompt: Why does asking a model to show its steps on a multi-step calculation often change whether the final answer is correct, not just how transparent it is?

options.label: Each generated intermediate step becomes real context the next step is predicted from, instead of the model having to get the whole calculation right in one continuous leap
Showing steps makes the model apply more computational effort behind the scenes
It doesn't actually change the answer, only its presentation

questions.explanation: Generating the steps is how the calculation gets done more reliably — each correct intermediate result becomes checkable context for the next prediction, rather than an invisible thing the model has to get right silently.

questions.from: This module — Making It Show Its Work
questions.prompt: A model's reasoning is four confident, well-organized paragraphs with no specific numbers or named assumptions in it. What's the actual problem with this as 'shown reasoning'?

options.label: It's fluent and on-topic but has nothing specific in it a person could independently check or challenge
It's too short to count as real reasoning
The model is deliberately concealing the real numbers

questions.explanation: Detailed and checkable are different properties — verifiable reasoning names its specific inputs and assumptions explicitly; confident prose about the topic doesn't.

questions.from: This module — Making It Show Its Work
questions.prompt: A reasoning chain has one early arithmetic slip; every step after it is internally consistent with that wrong number. Why does the final answer still look just as confident as a fully correct chain?

options.label: Internal consistency (each step correctly following the last) is a different property from correctness (each step being actually right) — fluent reasoning only guarantees the first
The model deliberately hides the error once it's made
This kind of error only happens when reasoning isn't shown

questions.explanation: A chain can be coherent, with every step correctly following the one before it, while still being wrong overall, because an early step's specific value was wrong.

questions.from: This module — Making It Show Its Work
questions.prompt: A model asked to double-check a fabricated citation confidently reaffirms it as accurate. Why doesn't self-review catch this?

options.label: Self-review can help with self-contained calculation slips, but it has no access to external ground truth — asking again just produces another prediction from the same ungrounded process
The model refuses to double-check factual claims
Self-review only works when explicitly labeled 'fact-check' rather than 'double-check'

questions.explanation: Self-review is a real but limited tool: useful for a second independent pass at internal logic, useless for manufacturing access to a fact the model never reliably had, since no external source gets consulted.

questions.from: Previous module — Getting Output You Can Use
questions.prompt: A prompt asks for 'a table' and it pastes into a plain-text field as raw pipe characters. What's the actual issue?

options.label: The prompt specified a shape but not the destination's rendering capability — markdown syntax needs a renderer the field doesn't have
The model produced broken markdown
Tables can never be pasted anywhere outside a markdown tool

questions.explanation: Naming the destination's actual required syntax (TSV, CSV, plain text) fixes this — the markdown itself was correctly formed.

questions.from: Previous module — Getting Output You Can Use
questions.prompt: Why does 'exactly 50 words' tend to produce more variation in actual length than 'under 60 words'?

options.label: An exact count requires landing precisely on a number while generating, which is harder than just staying under a ceiling
The two instructions are functionally identical
Exact counts are always honored perfectly in practice

questions.explanation: Treat an exact-count instruction as a rough target — an upper bound holds up more reliably because it only requires staying on one side of a boundary.

questions.from: Previous module — Getting Output You Can Use
questions.prompt: A structured-extraction prompt looks flawless in 10 manual tests, then shows a real failure rate at 1,000 runs. What does this actually demonstrate?

options.label: A small manual sample can hide a real, low-single-digit failure rate that only becomes statistically visible at volume
The model's reliability degrades the longer it runs
The 1,000-run version must have used a worse prompt

questions.explanation: Ten clean tests show a prompt isn't obviously broken; they don't prove the failure rate is zero — testing at real volume is what surfaces a small but real rate.

questions.from: Previous module — Getting Output You Can Use
questions.prompt: Why is naming exact allowed values for a restricted field (e.g. 'sentiment: exactly positive, negative, or neutral, lowercase') important for a downstream script?

options.label: Without it, casing or wording can drift between runs and silently break an exact-match filter downstream
It makes the model respond faster
It's a cosmetic best practice with no functional effect

questions.explanation: A vague field description gets reinterpreted differently each run; naming exact allowed values removes that specific ambiguity.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — The Anatomy of a Prompt
questions.prompt: What are the four components of a well-built prompt?

options.label: Task, context, constraints, format
Persona, tone, length, greeting
Question, hint, answer, example

questions.explanation: Task, context, constraints, and format — the framework every later module in this phase builds on.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Teaching by Example
questions.prompt: Why can a large, internally consistent example set outweigh a short instruction that contradicts it?

options.label: A large uniform example set is a strong repeated pattern in the context, and there's no fixed rule that a short instruction always wins over it
Instructions are always ignored whenever any examples are present
Example sets over ten items exceed a hard technical limit

questions.explanation: Examples and instructions are both just tokens shaping the next prediction — a large, consistent example block is a strong signal that can beat a short, conflicting instruction.

contentSections.body: A checkpoint that surfaces a wrong answer isn't a failure — it's telling you exactly what to re-read before the next module builds on it.

title: Why the first prompt is rarely the best one
description: A first-draft prompt reflects what you thought you needed before you'd seen any output — treating it as a draft, not a final answer, is the actual skill this whole module builds on.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a prompt's first draft typically underperforms a revised version, structurally, not just by chance
Identify specific gaps a first output reveals that the original prompt couldn't have anticipated

contentSections.title: You didn't know what you needed until you saw what you got

contentSections.body: A marketer writes a prompt for social captions, gets ten back, and only on reading them does she notice: six of them use an em dash in a way she actually dislikes, three are the right length and four run long, and none of them mention the seasonal angle she meant to imply but never actually wrote into the prompt. None of this was visible to her before she saw the first batch — she didn't know to specify 'no em dashes' because she didn't know that was going to be the model's default habit.

contentSections.question: Why couldn't she have caught these three issues by thinking harder about the prompt before running it?
contentSections.answer: Two of the three issues (the em dash habit, the length drift) are facts about how the model tends to respond to this specific prompt — information that doesn't exist until there's an actual output to look at. The third (the missing seasonal angle) was a gap in her own thinking that seeing ten caption-shaped outputs, none of which had it, made suddenly obvious in a way that staring at the prompt alone hadn't.
contentSections.hint: Some of what a first output reveals is about the model's tendencies; some of it is about a gap in the writer's own thinking that only becomes visible once she's looking at something concrete instead of an abstract plan.

contentSections.body:
A first-draft prompt is written with the best information available at the time: what you think you need, described as clearly as you can manage, based on nothing but your own head. That's a real limitation, not a lack of effort — some of what a prompt actually needs to specify only becomes visible once there's a real output to react to. You don't know the model's default habit for this particular request until you've seen it default to something. You don't always know exactly what you meant by 'seasonal angle' until you're looking at ten captions that don't have one and can suddenly point at the gap.

This is why treating a first prompt as a draft — something you expect to revise once, informed by real output, not something you're supposed to get right by thinking hard enough in advance — isn't a lower standard. It's a more accurate model of where the useful information actually comes from. The revision isn't a sign the first attempt failed; it's the step where information that genuinely didn't exist before the first run becomes available.

contentSections.scenario: A first prompt for weekly report summaries produces output that's accurate but noticeably repeats the same three opening phrases across different weeks' reports — something invisible from reading the prompt alone, obvious once several outputs sit side by side.
contentSections.question: What category of gap does this repetition reveal?

options.label: A pattern only visible across multiple outputs — no single run would show it, since it's about variation (or the lack of it) between runs, not a flaw in any individual output
A factual error in the report content
A sign the prompt should be discarded and rewritten from nothing

feedback.cross-run-pattern: Right — this specific gap couldn't show up in a single output, however carefully read, because it's about how outputs relate to *each other* across runs. Seeing multiple real outputs side by side is what makes a cross-run pattern like repeated phrasing visible at all.
feedback.factual-error: The reports are described as accurate — the issue here is about a stylistic pattern (repeated phrasing), not a wrong fact anywhere in any individual report.
feedback.start-over: A repeated-phrasing pattern is a specific, addressable gap ('vary the opening, don't default to the same three phrases') — it points to a targeted fix, not a signal that the whole prompt approach failed and needs to be abandoned.

contentSections.concept: Some gaps in a prompt are only visible across multiple real outputs, not from any single one

contentSections.body: A prompt's first output isn't a verdict on whether the prompt worked — it's the first piece of information that makes revising it possible at all.

contentSections.title: Revision as the actual skill, not a fallback

contentSections.body: Two people building the same recurring prompt: one treats getting it right on the first try as the goal, gets discouraged when it isn't, and either abandons the approach or keeps re-writing from scratch. The other expects a first draft, runs it, reads the output specifically looking for gaps, and makes one targeted change. The second person consistently ends up with a better prompt, faster — not because they're more talented at writing prompts, but because they're doing the actual skill this module is about.

contentSections.question: Both people hit the same first-draft result. What's the actual difference in what they do next that explains why the second one ends up with a better prompt, faster?
contentSections.answer: The first person treats the first output as a verdict — good or bad — and either stops or starts over from nothing. The second treats it as a source of specific, targeted information, reads it for gaps, and changes only what the gaps point to. The second approach reuses everything that already worked in the first draft instead of discarding it.
contentSections.hint: One of them is starting over each time something isn't perfect. What does the other one keep, and what does the other one change?

contentSections.body:
Treating the first prompt as good-until-proven-otherwise sets up a false pass/fail frame — either it worked (relief, stop) or it didn't (frustration, start over). Treating it as a draft you expect to revise sets up a different, more productive frame: run it, read the output specifically for gaps rather than judging it on a scale of good-to-bad, and make one change targeted at whatever specific gap you found. That's not a consolation process for people who didn't write a good enough prompt the first time — it's the actual mechanism by which any prompt that matters gets built, because the information a revision needs literally doesn't exist until there's a real output to learn from.

The rest of this module is about doing that revision process rigorously instead of by vibes: changing one thing at a time so you know what caused an improvement, testing against a fixed set of your own hard cases instead of a fresh example every time, and having an actual way to judge whether version two is better than version one instead of just feeling like it probably is.
The first prompt isn't supposed to be the final one — expecting to revise, informed by a real output, is the actual skill, not a sign the first attempt fell short.

title: Changing one thing at a time
description: Changing several parts of a prompt at once might produce a better result, but it leaves you with no way to know which change actually did it — which matters the next time something breaks.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why changing multiple prompt elements simultaneously undermines learning from the result
Isolate a single variable to change when revising an underperforming prompt

contentSections.title: Better, but why?

contentSections.body: A prompt for drafting apology emails to delayed customers isn't landing quite right — too stiff. In one pass, someone rewrites the tone instruction, adds two examples, and shortens the length constraint, all at once. The new version is noticeably better. Three weeks later, a different task needs the same tone fix, and there's no way to tell which of the three changes actually mattered — so all three get copied over out of caution, including two that were probably dead weight.

contentSections.scenario: Three changes were made simultaneously (tone instruction, examples added, length shortened) and the output improved. It's now unclear which change caused the improvement.
contentSections.question: What's actually lost by changing three things at once, even though the result was genuinely better?

options.label: The ability to attribute the improvement to a specific cause — meaning the lesson can't be reliably reused, isolated, or trusted the next time a similar problem shows up
Nothing is lost — a better result is a better result regardless of how many things changed
The prompt becomes permanently unfixable

feedback.no-attribution: Right — the immediate result (a better prompt for this one task) is real, but the reusable knowledge (which change actually fixed the tone problem) is gone. That's the real cost: not this prompt, but every future situation where knowing the actual cause would have saved time.
feedback.nothing-lost: The output itself is fine — what's lost is diagnostic information for next time. A single success with an unclear cause is a worse foundation to build on than the same success with a known cause.
feedback.unfixable: The prompt itself works fine going forward — it's not broken. What's broken is the ability to explain *why* it works, which is a different and separately costly problem.

contentSections.mechanism: Changing multiple variables at once can produce a better result while destroying the information about which variable actually caused it

contentSections.body:
This is the same logic as a controlled experiment, applied to a prompt: if you change the tone instruction, add examples, and shorten the length constraint all in the same revision, and the output improves, you genuinely don't know which of the three did the work — maybe all three contributed, maybe one did everything and the other two were irrelevant or even slightly counterproductive on their own. That's fine if this prompt is a one-off you'll never touch again. It's a real cost if this is a prompt you'll revise again, reuse elsewhere, or need to explain to someone else — because the actual cause of the improvement is now unknown, and unknown causes can't be applied anywhere else with any confidence.

Changing one thing at a time is slower per revision cycle and faster overall, because every revision teaches you something reusable: “examples fixed the tone problem, the length change didn't matter” is knowledge you can carry into the next prompt. Three simultaneous changes and a vague sense that it's better now teaches you nothing you can reuse.
A better result from multiple simultaneous changes is still a real improvement — it's just an improvement you can't learn anything reusable from.

contentSections.title: Picking which one thing to change

contentSections.body: Facing an underperforming prompt with several plausible things wrong with it — vague tone, no examples, unclear length — the temptation is to fix all of them at once, since they're all genuinely worth fixing eventually. The discipline is picking the one most likely to be the actual cause of the specific problem you're seeing, testing that alone, and only then moving to the next.

contentSections.question: A prompt for internal meeting-note summaries is too long and includes irrelevant small talk from the transcript. Put these revision steps in the order the one-change-at-a-time discipline actually requires.
steps: Identify the single most likely cause of the specific problem observed (no length constraint AND no instruction to exclude small talk are both plausible — pick the one you think is more likely to be the actual cause)
Change only that one element, leaving everything else in the prompt untouched
Re-run the prompt on the same test case and compare the new output specifically against the problem you were trying to fix
If the problem is fixed, stop or move to the next distinct issue; if it isn't, revert that change and try the other candidate instead
contentSections.explanation: This is the actual discipline: pick one candidate cause, change only that, test against the same case, and let the result tell you whether that was the real cause — rather than changing both the length instruction and the small-talk-exclusion instruction at once and never finding out which one (or both, or neither) actually mattered. If the first guess doesn't fix it, the discipline is reverting that change before trying the next one, not stacking a second change on top of an unconfirmed first one.

contentSections.body: When several things are plausibly wrong, fix the one you think is most likely responsible first, test it alone, and only move to the next after you know whether the first one actually mattered.

title: A test set of your own hard cases
description: Testing a revised prompt on a fresh, easy example every time hides regressions — a fixed set of your own genuinely hard cases, reused every time, is what actually catches them.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why testing on a new example each time fails to catch a prompt regressing on a previously-working case
Build a small, fixed test set that includes the genuinely hard cases a task will actually encounter

contentSections.title: It got better on the new example. Did it get worse on the old one?

contentSections.body: A prompt is revised to handle a tricky ambiguous case better. Tested on a new, similarly tricky example, it works great — success, ship it. Two weeks later someone notices the revised prompt now mishandles a straightforward case the original version handled fine, because the fix for the tricky case introduced an instruction that quietly confused the simple one. Nobody caught this, because nobody re-tested the simple case after the revision — only the new one.

contentSections.scenario: A prompt revision was tested only on the specific new case it was designed to fix, and passed. A previously-working simple case silently regressed and wasn't caught until it showed up in real use.
contentSections.question: What's the actual gap in the testing process here?

options.label: Testing a revision only on the new case it targets checks for improvement but not for regression — nothing verified the previously-working cases still worked after the change
The revision itself was fundamentally flawed and shouldn't have been attempted
This kind of regression is unpredictable and can't be caught by any testing process

feedback.no-regression-check: Right — the revision was tested against exactly one thing: does it fix the case it was meant to fix. Nothing checked whether it broke something that used to work. That's a gap in the testing process, not a flaw in the idea of revising the prompt at all.
feedback.flawed-revision: The revision correctly fixed the case it targeted — the problem isn't that the fix was wrong, it's that its side effect on a different case went unchecked, which is a testing gap, not a flaw in the fix itself.
feedback.unpredictable: This is exactly the kind of thing a fixed, reused test set is built to catch — it's not unpredictable in principle, it's uncaught because the simple case was never re-run after the change.

contentSections.mechanism: Testing a revision only on the case it's meant to fix checks for improvement but leaves regression on other cases completely uncaught

contentSections.body:
A single new test example can tell you a revision fixed the thing it was aimed at. It can't tell you anything about whether that same revision broke something else, because it's the only thing being checked. This is exactly why a fixed, reused test set matters more than it might seem to at first: every time a prompt is revised, re-running the *entire* set — not just the new case that motivated the change — is what would have caught the simple case quietly breaking. Without that, a revision's side effects on cases you're not actively thinking about are invisible until they show up somewhere real, later, disconnected from the change that actually caused them.

This is the direct payoff of building a test set once and reusing it every time, instead of testing fresh each round: the set becomes a standing check against regression, not just a one-time confirmation that today's fix worked.

contentSections.code: A team revises a customer-email prompt to better handle an angry-customer edge case, tests the revision only against a new angry-customer example, confirms it works well, and ships the change.
contentSections.question: What's missing from this process?

options.label: Re-running the previously-established test cases (calm inquiries, routine requests, other edge cases already handled) to check the revision didn't break something that used to work
A second angry-customer example, since one isn't enough to test that case
Nothing — testing the specific case being fixed is sufficient

feedback.rerun-existing: Right — confirming the targeted fix works is necessary but not sufficient. Re-running the full existing test set is what would catch a regression on a case the team wasn't specifically thinking about when they made this change.
feedback.second-angry-example: More coverage of the same case type doesn't address the actual gap, which is about *other*, previously-working cases — not about needing more evidence for the case that was already confirmed fixed.
feedback.sufficient: This is the exact gap the lesson identifies — testing only the targeted case checks for improvement, not for regression on everything else.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix: maintain a running test set of real cases (including the ones already handled well) and re-run the entire set, not just the new case, every time the prompt changes — this is what catches a fix for one problem quietly breaking something else.

contentSections.body: Testing only the case you just fixed tells you the fix worked. Re-running your whole test set is what tells you it didn't break something else.

contentSections.title: Building the set with the hard cases in it

contentSections.body: A test set that's ten variations of the same easy, typical case is nearly as blind as no test set at all — it'll pass every time and never catch anything, because it never contains the kind of input that actually breaks a prompt. The set has to include the genuinely hard, ambiguous, or edge-case inputs the task will really encounter, the same discipline from the examples module applied to testing instead of teaching.

contentSections.scenario: Building a 6-case test set for a prompt that classifies incoming support tickets by urgency (low/medium/high).
contentSections.question: Which of these belong in a genuinely useful test set (versus padding it with more of the same)?

items.label: One clearly high-urgency ticket (production outage, all users affected)
A second, nearly identical clearly-high-urgency ticket
A ticket that's genuinely arguable between medium and high urgency
A low-actual-impact ticket from a high-profile customer (tests whether urgency tracks actual impact, not customer prominence)
A ticket with garbled or incomplete text, testing how the prompt handles genuinely bad input

explanation.clear-high: Worth including once, as a sanity-check anchor case — if this ever fails, something is badly broken.
explanation.another-clear-high: This doesn't add new coverage — it's the same case type as the first clear-high example, testing nothing the first one didn't already test.
explanation.boundary-med-high: A genuinely arguable case is exactly where a prompt is likely to actually fail or behave inconsistently — this is high-value test coverage.
explanation.vip-low-impact: This tests a specific, realistic failure mode (urgency inflated by customer status rather than actual impact) that a set of only clear-cut cases would never surface.
explanation.malformed: Real input is messy — a test set with only clean, well-formed tickets will never reveal how the prompt handles the genuinely bad input it will eventually receive in production.

contentSections.synthesis: A useful test set is small but deliberately hard: one or two anchor cases to sanity-check nothing is badly broken, plus several genuine boundary and edge cases chosen specifically because they're where a prompt is likely to actually fail — not padded out with more instances of the case that was never going to be the problem.

contentSections.body: A test set of ten easy cases catches nothing. A test set of five genuinely hard ones, reused on every revision, is what actually protects a prompt over time.

title: Judging two outputs against a written rubric
description: Comparing two prompt versions by gut feeling ('this one seems better') is unreliable and hard to explain to anyone else — a written rubric, decided before you look at the outputs, fixes both problems.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an unwritten, after-the-fact judgment of 'which output is better' is an unreliable basis for choosing between prompt versions
Write a rubric with concrete, checkable criteria to judge between two prompt versions before looking at their outputs

contentSections.title: 'This one just reads better' isn't a reason you can reuse

contentSections.body: Two versions of a product description prompt are run side by side. Someone reads both and picks version B: “yeah, this one just reads better.” Asked why, three different reasonable-sounding justifications come out in the next thirty seconds — B is punchier, B mentions the price sooner, B doesn't repeat a word — none of which were decided *before* reading the outputs, all of which sound plausible after the fact.

contentSections.scenario: A judgment of 'B is better' was made first, and the specific reasons were generated afterward, on demand, when asked to justify it.
contentSections.question: What's the actual risk in reasons that get generated after the preference, rather than criteria set before it?

options.label: After-the-fact reasons tend to rationalize a gut preference rather than actually having caused it — which means the same person comparing the same two outputs on a different day, in a different mood, could easily land on the opposite preference with an equally plausible-sounding justification
There's no real risk — any reasonable-sounding justification is just as valid as a pre-decided one
The specific reasons given (punchier, mentions price sooner) must be wrong since they came second

feedback.post-hoc-rationalization: Right — this is the core problem with judging by unreflective preference: the reasons offered afterward may or may not be what actually drove the preference, and there's no way to tell, which means the judgment isn't reliably reproducible even by the same person.
feedback.no-risk: The risk is real and specific: a preference formed before any stated criteria is much less stable and much less explainable to someone else than one measured against criteria decided in advance.
feedback.reasons-wrong: The individual reasons might all be genuinely true observations about the two outputs — the issue isn't that they're false, it's that they weren't what the comparison was actually built around, so a different comparison could reasonably surface different, equally true-sounding reasons pointing the other way.

contentSections.mechanism: Reasons generated to justify an already-formed preference are less reliable and less reproducible than criteria decided before the comparison

contentSections.body:
This isn't a claim that gut reactions to writing are worthless — a reader's instinct that something reads better often does track something real. The problem is specifically using that instinct as the entire basis for a decision, with no criteria fixed beforehand, because the explanation that follows is being constructed to justify a conclusion that's already been reached, not discovered independently of it. That's a shaky foundation for a decision you might need to defend, repeat consistently, or hand off to someone else to apply the same way.

The fix is deciding the criteria before looking at the two outputs: what, specifically, makes a product description for this store better — mentions the price, states the material, stays under 50 words, doesn't use the phrase 'crystal-clear.' Written down first, those criteria turn 'B just reads better' into 'B meets 4 of 5 criteria, A meets 2' — a comparison a different person, or the same person on a different day, could redo and land on the same answer.
A preference explained after the fact tends to justify itself, not test itself — decide what 'better' means before you look at the two outputs, not after.

contentSections.title: Building the rubric

contentSections.body: Before comparing two versions of the support-ticket urgency classifier from the previous lesson, a rubric gets written first: correctly identifies genuine high-urgency cases, doesn't inflate urgency for high-profile customers with low actual impact, handles the boundary case consistently, produces output in the exact required format. Four concrete, checkable items — decided before either version's output is read.

contentSections.intro: Build a rubric to compare two versions of a prompt that summarizes long customer support call transcripts into 3-bullet summaries for a manager.

options: Captures the actual resolution or next step, not just the complaint
Uses professional-sounding vocabulary
Is written in complete sentences
fields.correctValue: Captures the actual resolution or next step, not just the complaint
fields.feedback: This is concrete and checkable — you can look at a summary and determine yes/no whether the resolution is present. 'Professional-sounding' and 'complete sentences' are either not the actual point of a bulleted summary or too vague to check reliably.

options: Exactly 3 bullets, each under 20 words
Sounds engaging
Uses varied vocabulary
fields.feedback: A concrete count-and-length check, directly verifiable by looking at the output — unlike 'sounds engaging,' which is exactly the kind of vibe-word this module is steering away from as a criterion.

options: Doesn't include the customer's raw emotional language verbatim (paraphrases frustration rather than quoting it)
Is shorter than the original transcript
Mentions the agent's name
fields.correctValue: Doesn't include the customer's raw emotional language verbatim (paraphrases frustration rather than quoting it)
fields.feedback: This is a specific, real editorial standard a manager reading these would care about and that's directly checkable. 'Shorter than the original' is trivially true of any summary and not a meaningful discriminator; the agent's name isn't relevant to summary quality.

options: Correctly identifies which of multiple issues raised in the call was the primary one, when more than one was discussed
Is grammatically perfect
Starts with the customer's name
fields.correctValue: Correctly identifies which of multiple issues raised in the call was the primary one, when more than one was discussed
fields.feedback: This targets a real, checkable judgment call the summarization task actually has to get right — grammar and a naming convention are much lower-value, less discriminating criteria for comparing two prompt versions on this task.

contentSections.synthesis: A working rubric for this task: captures the actual resolution, exactly 3 bullets under 20 words each, paraphrases rather than quotes raw emotional language, and correctly identifies the primary issue among several. Each is something you could look at either version's output and mark yes or no on — which is what makes the eventual comparison ('version B meets 4 of 4, version A meets 2 of 4') something someone else could redo and land on the same conclusion.

contentSections.body: A good rubric item is something you could look at an output and mark yes or no on — if a criterion needs a vibe check to apply, it's not doing the job a rubric is for.

title: Knowing when it's good enough to stop
description: Iteration has a real cost — every revision cycle takes time — and a prompt that's good enough for its actual stakes doesn't need to be perfect for stakes it doesn't have.

learningObjectives.text: Judge whether a prompt's current performance is sufficient for its actual stakes, rather than defaulting to further iteration
Identify diminishing returns in a prompt's revision history

contentSections.title: Good enough for what, exactly

contentSections.body: A prompt for drafting first-pass replies to routine, low-stakes internal Slack questions — “what's our PTO policy” type things, always reviewed by a person before sending — is at 90% rubric compliance after two revision rounds. A prompt for drafting the first pass of a legal disclaimer that ships unreviewed to customers is also at 90% after two rounds. Treating both as equally 'good enough to ship' misses something obvious about what's actually at stake in each.

contentSections.scenario: Two prompts at the same 90% rubric-compliance score, with very different consequences if the remaining 10% of cases go wrong.
contentSections.question: What should actually determine whether 90% is 'good enough to stop iterating' for a given prompt?

options.label: The real-world cost of the failure cases in that remaining 10% — a reviewed, low-stakes draft can tolerate a rough edge that an unreviewed, higher-stakes one can't
A fixed universal threshold — 90% is always good enough, regardless of what the prompt is for
Whichever prompt was iterated on for more total rounds should be trusted more

feedback.cost-of-failure: Right — the same percentage means something very different depending on what happens when it's wrong. A human-reviewed low-stakes draft can absorb an occasional rough output; an unreviewed high-stakes one, at the same failure rate, is shipping errors directly to customers with no safety net.
feedback.fixed-threshold: There's no single number that's correct regardless of context — a 90% score is a genuinely different situation depending on what a failure actually costs, not a pass/fail line by itself.
feedback.rounds-count: The number of revision rounds already invested doesn't determine whether the current version is adequate for its actual stakes — that's a sunk-cost framing, not a stakes-based one.

contentSections.concept: The bar for 'good enough' is set by the real cost of failure, not by a fixed score or by how much revision has already happened

contentSections.body:
A rubric score or a measured accuracy number is genuinely useful information, but it isn't, by itself, a stopping rule — “good enough” has to be defined against what actually happens when the remaining failure cases occur. A prompt whose output a human reviews before it goes anywhere can tolerate a real, nonzero failure rate, because the review is the actual safety net. A prompt whose output goes straight to a customer, a legal document, or an automated decision with no human in the loop needs a much higher bar, or needs a human-in-the-loop step added, because there's nothing else catching the failure cases.

This cuts both ways. It's just as much a mistake to keep iterating a low-stakes, human-reviewed prompt for a fourth and fifth round chasing marginal gains as it is to ship a high-stakes, unreviewed one after two rounds because the score looked fine. Knowing when to stop requires knowing what the actual downstream stakes are, not just what the current score is.
The same score means different things at different stakes — set the bar for 'good enough' based on what happens when the remaining failures actually occur, not on the number alone.

contentSections.title: Diminishing returns, named honestly

contentSections.body: A prompt's rubric score across four revision rounds: 60%, 82%, 89%, 90%. The jump from round 1 to round 2 was large and easy to attribute to a clear fix. The jump from round 3 to round 4 was one point, after a genuinely thoughtful change, and cost the same amount of time as the much bigger early jumps.

contentSections.scenario: Continuing to iterate the same prompt for a fifth round, with the same level of effort as previous rounds.
contentSections.question: Based on the pattern across rounds 1 through 4, roughly how many more percentage points would a typical fifth round of similar effort be expected to add?
contentSections.explanation: Following the same diminishing pattern visible from round 1 to round 4 (22 points, then 7, then 1), a fifth round of similar effort would typically be expected to add somewhere around zero to one or two more points, not another large jump — the pattern strongly suggests the easy, high-leverage fixes are already made, and what's left is the genuinely hard-to-close residual gap, which usually needs a different kind of intervention (a different technique entirely, or accepting a human-review step) rather than another round of the same kind of tweaking.

contentSections.body:
A revision history with diminishing returns isn't a sign iteration has stopped working — it's the expected shape of the process, and recognizing the shape is what tells you when to stop applying more of the same kind of effort. The early rounds fix the big, obvious gaps (missing structure, a vague instruction, an unhandled edge case) and produce large jumps. The later rounds are chasing smaller and smaller gaps, and the same size of effort buys less and less. Continuing to iterate identically past that point isn't wrong exactly, but it's spending real time for a return that's shrinking toward zero — worth noticing honestly rather than continuing on autopilot because 'iterating more' feels like the responsible thing to keep doing.

When the returns have genuinely flattened and the score still isn't high enough for the task's actual stakes, that's a signal to consider a different lever entirely — a different technique from this whole module (examples, decomposition, structured output), not just another round of the same kind of tweak — or to add a safety net downstream (validation, human review) rather than trying to close the last gap with prompt wording alone.
A flattening revision curve isn't failure — it's the signal that the easy fixes are already made, and it's time to either change technique, add a downstream safety net, or genuinely stop.

title: Practice — Diagnose and Fix Eight Failing Prompts
description: Eight drills on isolating the right variable to change, building a real test set, judging by rubric instead of gut feeling, and knowing when a prompt is genuinely good enough. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose the most likely single cause of a prompt's specific failure
Judge whether a prompt's measured performance is adequate for its actual stakes

contentSections.title: Eight iteration judgment calls

contentSections.body: Eight quick scenarios about revising a prompt the way this module actually teaches — one change at a time, tested against real cases, judged against a written rubric, stopped at the right point.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Improve One Prompt Across Three Measured Rounds
description: Take a real, currently-imperfect prompt through three genuine, evidence-based revision rounds — one change at a time, scored against a fixed test set and a written rubric.

learningObjectives.text: Revise a prompt across multiple rounds, changing one variable per round and measuring the result
Judge when a prompt's measured performance is adequate to stop iterating

contentSections.title: Three real rounds, each one measured

contentSections.body: Pick a real prompt you'd actually use again — ideally one you already know has some rough edges — for a task with a genuine right-or-wrong-ish answer you could build a rubric around: a classification task, a formatting task, a summarization task with clear required content.

contentSections.title: Three prompt versions, scored against a fixed test set, with a written conclusion
contentSections.brief: Choose a real, currently-imperfect prompt and build a fixed test set of 5-8 cases, including at least 2-3 genuinely hard or boundary cases, plus a written rubric of 4-6 concrete, checkable criteria — both decided before you look at any output. Score version 1 against the full test set and rubric. Then run three rounds of revision, each changing exactly one thing based on what the previous round's failures actually showed, re-scoring the FULL test set (not just the case that motivated the change) after each round.
contentSections.deliverable: The test set, the rubric, all three (or four, including the original) prompt versions, their scores against the full test set and rubric each round, and a written conclusion stating the final score, whether it's adequate for this prompt's actual real-world stakes, and what you'd do next if it isn't.

stages.title: Build the test set, rubric, and baseline
stages.instructions: Gather 5-8 real or realistic test cases including at least 2-3 genuinely hard or boundary ones. Write a rubric of 4-6 concrete, checkable criteria — decide these before running anything. Score your current (version 1) prompt against the full test set and rubric, and note specifically which criteria failed on which cases.
stages.checkpoint: You have a fixed test set, a written rubric, and version 1's score with specific documented failures.

stages.title: Round 2: one change, full re-test
stages.instructions: Based on version 1's most common or most important failure, make exactly one change to the prompt. Re-run the FULL test set (all 5-8 cases, not just the ones that failed before) and re-score against the same rubric.
stages.checkpoint: You have version 2's full score, and you can name specifically what changed and whether it helped, hurt, or had no effect on each previously-failing case — and whether anything that previously passed now fails.

stages.title: Round 3: one more change, full re-test
stages.instructions: Based on version 2's remaining failures, make exactly one more change (not a combination of several). Re-run the full test set again and re-score.
stages.checkpoint: You have version 3's full score, with the same before/after tracking as round 2.

stages.title: Conclude
stages.instructions: Write a short conclusion: the score trajectory across all three (or four) versions, whether the returns are flattening, whether the final score is adequate given this prompt's actual real-world stakes, and — if it isn't adequate yet — what you'd do differently next (a different technique, or a downstream safety net) rather than just another round of the same kind of tweak.
stages.checkpoint: You have a written conclusion naming the score trajectory, a stakes-based judgment of adequacy, and a specific next step if the prompt isn't there yet.

rubric.criterion: The test set and rubric were both fixed before any output was judged
rubric.meets: Test cases and rubric criteria are dated/ordered before the first scoring pass, not adjusted afterward to match what happened to work.

rubric.criterion: The test set includes genuine hard cases, not just easy ones
rubric.meets: At least 2-3 of the test cases are ones a real deployment would find genuinely ambiguous or difficult.

rubric.criterion: Each revision round changed exactly one thing
rubric.meets: Each round's change can be described as a single, specific modification, not a bundle of several simultaneous changes.

rubric.criterion: The FULL test set was re-scored every round, not just the motivating case
rubric.meets: All rounds' scores cover every case in the test set, including ones that weren't the target of that round's change — so a regression would actually be visible.

rubric.criterion: The rubric criteria are concrete and checkable
rubric.meets: Each criterion could be marked yes/no by looking at an output, without needing a subjective vibe judgment.

rubric.criterion: The conclusion makes a stakes-based adequacy judgment, not just a score report
rubric.meets: The write-up states whether the final score is good enough for this prompt's actual real-world consequences, not just what the number is.

contentSections.body: Three genuinely measured rounds — one change, full re-test, real rubric, every time — teach you more about a prompt than a dozen rounds of tweaking and eyeballing the result.

title: Checkpoint — Improving a Prompt Systematically
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Making It Show Its Work, two reaching further back to Teaching by Example.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the systematic-iteration judgment calls from this module and the reasoning-prompting judgment calls before it, without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Improving a Prompt Systematically

questions.from: This module — Improving a Prompt Systematically
questions.prompt: Why is a first-draft prompt's underperformance usually not a sign of insufficient effort?

options.label: Some of what a prompt needs to specify — the model's default habits, cross-run patterns, gaps only visible once there's real output — genuinely can't be known before a first output exists
First drafts are always written carelessly compared to revisions
Models perform worse on a prompt's first-ever run specifically

questions.explanation: A first draft reflects the best information available before any real output exists — some genuinely useful information only becomes visible after seeing what the model actually produces.

questions.from: This module — Improving a Prompt Systematically
questions.prompt: A revision changes three things at once and the output improves. What's actually lost, even though the result is genuinely better?

options.label: The ability to attribute the improvement to a specific cause, so the lesson can't be reliably reused elsewhere
Nothing — a better result is a better result regardless of how many things changed
The prompt becomes permanently unfixable

questions.explanation: Changing one thing at a time is what turns a revision into reusable knowledge about what actually causes what — bundled changes produce a real result with an unknown cause.

questions.from: This module — Improving a Prompt Systematically
questions.prompt: Why does testing a prompt revision only against the new case it was designed to fix leave a real gap?

options.label: It checks for improvement on the targeted case but leaves regression on previously-working cases completely uncaught
New test cases are always less reliable than old ones
There's no gap — testing the targeted case is sufficient

questions.explanation: Re-running the full, fixed test set — not just the motivating case — is what catches a fix for one problem quietly breaking something that used to work.

questions.from: This module — Improving a Prompt Systematically
questions.prompt: Two prompts both score 90% on their rubrics — one for a human-reviewed low-stakes draft, one for an unreviewed high-stakes document. Should both be treated as equally 'good enough to ship'?

options.label: No — the real cost of the remaining 10% of failures is very different in each case, and that cost, not the score alone, should set the bar for adequate
Yes — 90% is 90% regardless of context
No — the one iterated on for more rounds should always be trusted more

questions.explanation: The same score means different things depending on what happens when a failure occurs — a reviewed low-stakes draft can tolerate a rough edge an unreviewed high-stakes one can't.

questions.from: Previous module — Making It Show Its Work
questions.prompt: Why does asking a model to show its steps on a multi-step calculation often change whether the final answer is correct?

options.label: Each generated intermediate step becomes real context the next step is predicted from, instead of the model getting the whole calculation right in one leap
Showing steps applies more raw computational effort behind the scenes
It doesn't actually change the answer, only its presentation

questions.explanation: Generating the steps is how the calculation gets done more reliably — each step becomes checkable context for the next prediction.

questions.from: Previous module — Making It Show Its Work
questions.prompt: A reasoning chain has one early arithmetic slip; every step after it is internally consistent with that wrong number. Why does the final answer still look confident?

options.label: Internal consistency (each step following the last) is different from correctness (each step being actually right) — fluent reasoning only guarantees the first
The model deliberately conceals the error
This only happens in unshown reasoning

questions.explanation: A chain can be coherent while still being wrong overall, because an early step's specific value was wrong and everything after correctly builds on it.

questions.from: Previous module — Making It Show Its Work
questions.prompt: Why doesn't asking a model to 'double-check' a fabricated citation reliably catch the fabrication?

options.label: Self-review can help with self-contained calculation slips, but has no access to external ground truth for a specific real-world fact
Models refuse to double-check factual claims
It only works if the request specifically says 'fact-check' rather than 'double-check'

questions.explanation: No external source is consulted on a second pass any more than the first — self-review is bounded to internal-logic slips, not real-world fact verification.

questions.from: Previous module — Making It Show Its Work
questions.prompt: A single prompt bundles extracting pain points, ranking them, and writing a brief. Why is the ranking (middle step) often the weakest part?

options.label: There's no natural pause between the judgment step and the generation step — a rushed judgment can flow straight into confident-sounding prose built on top of it
Ranking is inherently harder than writing a brief
The model can only handle two bundled tasks reliably

questions.explanation: Splitting bundled tasks with a real judgment call in the middle creates a checkable intermediate result before building further output on top of it.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Teaching by Example
questions.prompt: Why can a large, internally consistent example set outweigh a short instruction that contradicts it?

options.label: A large uniform example set is a strong repeated pattern in the context — there's no fixed rule that a short instruction always wins
Instructions are always ignored whenever any examples are present
Example sets over ten items exceed a hard technical limit

questions.explanation: Examples and instructions are both just tokens shaping the next prediction — a large, consistent example block is a strong signal that can beat a short, conflicting instruction.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Teaching by Example
questions.prompt: Three feedback examples are all about environmental-topic essays, though topic was never the intended lesson. What's the risk?

options.label: The model may generalize the coincidental shared topic alongside the intended pattern, since it can't distinguish intentional from accidental consistency
There's no risk — the model only learns the intended lesson
The risk only applies with more than ten examples

questions.explanation: Every consistently-shared feature across an example set, intentional or not, is a candidate for what gets generalized — vary what you don't intend to teach.

contentSections.body: A checkpoint that surfaces a wrong answer isn't a failure — it's telling you exactly what to re-read before the next module, or the next phase, builds on it.
